title: Database Management & SQL
tagline: Design clean data, ask sharp questions in SQL, keep systems fast under load and protect every record: practical database skills for organisations anywhere.
sectors: Mobile money, wallets and payment providers
description:
Behind every account statement, mobile top-up, payroll run and board report sits a database. When it is designed well and run well, nobody notices. When it is not, customers are charged twice, reports disagree with the ledger, systems crawl on payday and a single bad night can wipe out hours of transactions.

This certification gives analysts, developers and IT staff the practical database skills that banks, telecoms, retailers and public bodies depend on, wherever they operate. You will model data with **entities, keys and normal forms**, write real **SQL** from `SELECT` and `JOIN` through `GROUP BY`, subqueries, CTEs and **window functions**, read execution plans and design **indexes**, and reason about **transactions, isolation and locking** when thousands of users hit the same rows.

You will also learn to protect the data: **backup and recovery** planned around RPO and RTO, **least privilege**, defences against **SQL injection**, encryption and masking, and the international principles behind data-protection laws from the EU to Singapore, Kenya and India. A light tour of data warehousing and NoSQL shows where the relational model fits in a modern data estate.

Every stage includes **real cases from around the world**, from a public-health spreadsheet that lost thousands of test results to a bitcoin bank emptied by a race condition. Five story stages, a ten-question test after each, and a tough timed final exam built on realistic scenarios.
audience: Data, MIS and business analysts who write SQL to produce reports and answer management questions
Application developers who design tables and write queries for core systems, apps and wallets
Database administrators and IT operations staff who keep production systems fast, safe and recoverable
Information security, IT audit and risk staff who review database controls
Technology graduates and career switchers preparing for data roles in any sector or country
outcomes: Model business data as entities, attributes and relationships, choose sound keys and normalise to third normal form
Write correct SQL with joins, aggregation, subqueries, CTEs and window functions, and avoid NULL and join fan-out traps
Diagnose slow queries using execution plans, sargable predicates and well-chosen composite and covering indexes
Explain ACID, isolation levels, locking and deadlocks, and design transactions that prevent double debits and lost updates
Plan backup and recovery against RPO and RTO targets, including restore chains and point-in-time recovery
Apply least privilege, injection-proof coding, encryption, masking and auditing, guided by international data-protection principles and the rules where you work
Decide when a data warehouse or a NoSQL store complements the relational core

quest.premise: Orvella Bank, a fast-growing digital bank run from Dubai with operations in the UK, Kenya, Singapore, Malaysia and Pakistan, is replacing fifteen years of patched-together databases and spreadsheets with a new core platform, Keystone, before the year-end payroll peak. You join the data platform team. With mentor Amara Okafor, developer Rafael Souza, analyst Layla Haddad, security officer Mei Tan and an impatient COO, Vikram Nair, clear five stages from a tangled legacy archive to a midnight recovery, then face the final boss: the go-live board review.

sessions.title: Designing the Data: Entities, Keys and Normal Forms
sessions.summary: Before Keystone can go live, the bank's tangled legacy customer table has to become a clean relational model. Learn to find entities, choose keys, draw relationships and normalise to third normal form.

cards.title: Day one: the table from the basement
cards.setting: Data platform floor, Orvella Bank's regional hub, Dubai. 9:10 am.

lines.text: Your access card works on the second try. Before your laptop has even booted, a printout lands on your desk.
Welcome to Operation Keystone. I'm Amara, I run data platforms. That printout is CUSTMAST, the customer table our old system has used since 2010.

Look at row 4,112. Columns ACCOUNT1, ACCOUNT2, ACCOUNT3. A phone column holding two numbers separated by a comma. And the same national ID number appears three times, spelled 'Muhammad', 'Muhammed' and 'M.'
Amara, I've seen the plan. Keystone goes live before the year-end payroll peak. Can't we just copy this table across and clean it later?
Copying a mess only moves the mess, Vikram. If Keystone inherits this design, every report and every wallet payment inherits it too.
I can confirm that. My branch deposit report and Finance's figure have not matched for two years. Nobody knows which one is right.
So your first mission is to design the customer and account data properly. What are the real things we store, how do we identify each one, and how do they connect?

cards.title: What a relational database really is

scenes.heading: Tables that mean something
scenes.narration: A relational database stores data in tables. Each table holds one kind of thing, such as customers, branches or accounts. Each row is one instance, and each column is one fact about it.

scenes.heading: Every row has an identity
scenes.narration: Every table has a primary key: a column, or a set of columns, whose value is unique and never empty. It lets you point at exactly one customer or exactly one account.

scenes.heading: Keys build the links
scenes.narration: Tables connect through foreign keys. An account row stores the customer ID of its owner, and the database refuses an account that points at a customer who does not exist.

scenes.heading: The engine enforces the rules
scenes.narration: A database management system, the DBMS, enforces keys, data types and constraints for every user and every application, so bad data is stopped at the door instead of cleaned up later.

scenes.heading: SQL is how you talk to it
scenes.narration: You define and query everything with SQL, the Structured Query Language. You describe the result you want, and the engine works out how to fetch it.

cards.title: Real case: the spreadsheet that lost nearly 16,000 test results
cards.body:
**England, October 2020.** Public Health England revealed that **15,841 positive COVID-19 test results**, recorded between 25 September and 2 October, had not reached the national contact-tracing system.

**What went wrong:**
- Labs sent results as text (CSV) files, which were loaded into Excel templates.
- The templates used the old **.xls format, which holds only about 65,000 rows** per sheet.
- When a file was bigger, the extra rows were **silently cut off**. No error, no warning.

The missing cases were added to the official figures a few days later, but contact tracing for thousands of people started late.

**The database lesson:** a spreadsheet is not a data pipeline. A proper load into a database rejects or reports what it cannot store, and a simple **control total** (rows received versus rows loaded) would have exposed the gap on day one.

cards.title: Keys you will use every day

cards.back: The column or columns chosen to identify each row. Must be unique and never NULL. One per table.
Any minimal set of columns that could uniquely identify a row. One becomes the primary key; the rest are alternate keys.
An identifier from the real world, such as a national ID number, an IBAN or a mobile number. Convenient, but it can change, be missing or be reused: telcos recycle numbers.
A meaningless value generated by the database, such as customer_id 100245. It never changes even when real-world details do.
A key made of two or more columns together, such as (account_id, customer_id) in a joint-holder table.
A column that must match a primary key in another table, so there are no orphan rows. Its ON DELETE rule sets what happens to children: RESTRICT blocks the delete, CASCADE deletes them too.
Guarantees no two rows share a value. Use it on a natural key, such as a national ID number, when a surrogate key is the PK.

cards.question: Keystone's accounts table stores customer_id for each account. A developer tries to insert an account with customer_id 999999, which does not exist in the customers table. What should happen if the model is built correctly?
options: The insert succeeds and the account is linked later during month-end clean-up
The database creates an empty customer 999999 automatically
The foreign key rejects the insert, because every account must point to an existing customer
The primary key on accounts rejects it, because account IDs must be unique
cards.explanation: A foreign key enforces referential integrity: the child row (account) must reference an existing parent row (customer). The primary key on accounts only guarantees that account IDs are unique; it says nothing about whether the customer exists.

cards.title: Entities, relationships and cardinality
cards.body:
An **entity** is a thing the business needs to remember: customer, branch, account, transaction. **Attributes** are its facts: name, city, opening date.

**Cardinality** says how many of one entity relate to another:
- **One-to-one (1:1):** one employee, one company laptop.
- **One-to-many (1:N):** one branch has many accounts. The foreign key goes on the **many** side: `accounts.branch_id`.
- **Many-to-many (M:N):** a customer can hold many accounts, and a joint account has many holders. A relational table cannot store this directly, so you add a **junction table**, `account_holders(account_id, customer_id, role)`, with a composite key.

**Optionality** says whether the link is required: every account **must** have a branch, but a customer **may** have no loan yet.

An **ER diagram** draws entities as boxes and relationships as lines, with symbols for "one", "many" and "optional" at each end. Draw it with the business before you write any table.

cards.title: Three ways a bad table bites
cards.setting: Layla's desk, MIS bay, 11:45 am. Three tickets are open on her screen.

lines.text: Ticket one: Ms Chen Wei moved from Penang to Kuala Lumpur. Operations updated her city on two CUSTMAST rows but missed the third. Now she is in two cities.
Ticket two: a customer closed her only account, the row was deleted, and her address and KYC details went with it.
Ticket three: our new Mombasa branch can't be added to the system until its first account is opened, because branch details live only on account rows.
Those are the three classic anomalies: update, delete and insert. They all come from one table trying to store facts about several different things.
So we split the table. But how do we know where to cut?
Normalisation. Each normal form is a test, and every failed test tells you exactly which columns to move.

cards.title: Climbing the normal forms
cards.caption: Each level assumes the one below it. For transaction systems, 3NF is the usual target.

items.label: BCNF
items.detail: Stricter 3NF: every determinant must be a candidate key. Rarely needed beyond 3NF in practice.

items.label: Third normal form (3NF)
items.detail: No non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency).

items.label: Second normal form (2NF)
items.detail: Every non-key column depends on the whole key, not part of a composite key.

items.label: First normal form (1NF)
items.detail: Atomic values in every cell; no repeating groups like ACCOUNT1, ACCOUNT2.

cards.title: The normal forms in plain words
cards.body:
A neat way to remember the target: every non-key column should depend on **the key, all of the key, and only the key**.

- **1NF: one value per cell, no repeating groups.** `phone = '+44 7700 900111, +44 7700 900222'` and columns `ACCOUNT1..ACCOUNT3` both fail. Fix: one row per phone or account in a separate table.
- **2NF: all of the key.** Only matters when the key is **composite**. In `loan_installments(loan_id, installment_no, due_date, borrower_name)` the borrower name depends on `loan_id` alone, which is a **partial dependency**. Move it to `loans`.
- **3NF: only the key.** In `accounts(account_id, branch_id, branch_city)`, `branch_city` depends on `branch_id`, not on the account. That is a **transitive dependency**. Move it to `branches`.

A table whose key is a single column cannot have a partial dependency, so if it is in 1NF it is automatically in 2NF.

cards.title: Which normal form does it break?
cards.prompt: Each legacy table design below breaks one normal form first. Sort it into the lowest form it violates.

items.text: CUSTMAST has columns ACCOUNT1, ACCOUNT2 and ACCOUNT3
account_holders(account_id, customer_id, role, customer_name) with key (account_id, customer_id)
loan_installments(loan_id, installment_no, due_date, loan_product_name) keyed on both IDs
bundle_subscriptions(msisdn, bundle_code, start_date, bundle_price) keyed on all three

cards.question: A design has accounts(account_id PK, customer_id, branch_id, branch_manager_name). Which problem does branch_manager_name create?
options: A partial dependency that breaks 2NF: it depends on part of the key
A transitive dependency that breaks 3NF: it depends on branch_id, not on the account
A repeating group that breaks 1NF
No problem, because the table has a single-column primary key
cards.explanation: The manager's name is a fact about the branch. It reaches the account only through branch_id, which is a transitive dependency, so it belongs in branches. 2NF cannot be broken here because the key is a single column.

cards.title: Copy now, clean later?
cards.situation: Vikram calls a meeting. Keystone's migration window is tight, and he proposes loading CUSTMAST into Keystone exactly as it is: repeating account columns, multi-value phone fields, 38,000 rows with duplicate national ID numbers and all. 'The vendor says we can fix the data in phase two.' Amara asks you to recommend a way forward.

choices.text: Agree. Phase two is only six months away, and meeting the year-end date matters most.
choices.outcome: Keystone launches with the old anomalies built in. Within weeks, wallet KYC checks fail on duplicate customers, and every new report needs workarounds. Phase two keeps slipping, because by then dozens of programs depend on the bad design.

choices.text: Model the core entities to 3NF, migrate through a staging area that deduplicates on national ID number, load rejects into an exceptions table for Operations, and enforce keys and constraints from day one.
choices.outcome: The migration takes one extra rehearsal, but Keystone starts clean. Operations works through 2,100 exception records with clear reasons attached, and the constraints stop new duplicates from appearing. This is the professional answer: fix the design at the door and manage the data clean-up as a tracked list.

choices.text: Flatten everything into one wide 'customer_360' table in Keystone, so queries never need joins.
choices.outcome: Reads are simple at first, but every change to a customer must now update many rows. Update anomalies return immediately, and the table grows wide and fragile. A wide table can serve reporting, but it is a poor master record for a bank.

choices.text: Delay go-live until every legacy record is perfectly cleaned, verified and normalised beyond 3NF.
choices.outcome: The design instinct is right, but perfection on legacy data never arrives, and the business misses the year-end window. A clean design plus a managed exceptions list would have met both goals.

cards.title: Normalising the legacy table
cards.prompt: Put Amara's normalisation routine for CUSTMAST in the right order.
steps: List every attribute in the legacy table and what each one means
Split out repeating groups and multi-value cells into their own tables (1NF)
Identify the key of each table and move columns that depend on only part of it (2NF)
Move columns that depend on other non-key columns into their own tables (3NF)
Declare primary keys, foreign keys, unique and check constraints
Load the data through staging, then reconcile row counts and totals against the old system

cards.title: Let constraints and types do free quality checks
cards.body:
- **NOT NULL** on facts that must exist, like an account's branch.
- **UNIQUE** on natural keys, such as a national ID.
- **CHECK** for allowed values: `CHECK (txn_type IN ('CR','DR'))`. Longer lists: a lookup table with a foreign key.
- **Money in DECIMAL**, for example `DECIMAL(18,2)`. Never FLOAT: binary floating point cannot store 0.10 exactly, and the pennies drift.
- **Identifiers as text** when you never do arithmetic on them. A phone number stored as an integer loses its leading zero.
- **Dates as DATE or TIMESTAMP**, never as text like '05/11/26'.
- **ON DELETE RESTRICT** on financial history. When merging duplicate customers, re-point child rows to the surviving record first.

cards.title: Real case: when spreadsheets renamed human genes
cards.body:
Gene symbols such as **SEPT2** (septin 2) and **MARCH1** look like dates to a spreadsheet, which helpfully turns them into 2-Sep and 1-Mar.

- **2016:** a study in the journal *Genome Biology* checked published papers whose supplementary data included gene lists in Excel. Roughly **one in five** contained gene names corrupted in this way.
- **2020:** the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee, which names human genes, **renamed 27 genes** (for example SEPT1 became SEPTIN1 and MARCH1 became MARCHF1), partly so they would stop being mangled.

The scientists had to change the data because the tool kept guessing types.

**The database lesson:** never let software guess. **Declare every column's type**, store identifiers as **text**, and add **CHECK** constraints for their format, so a value either goes in exactly as written or is rejected.

cards.title: Keystone's first three tables
cards.body:
Amara's team agrees this core model:

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  national_id  VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE,   -- NULL if no ID yet (see note)
  full_name    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  city         VARCHAR(40)
);
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  account_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  branch_id    INT NOT NULL REFERENCES branches(branch_id),
  opened_on    DATE NOT NULL,
  status       CHAR(1) NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('A','D','C'))
);
CREATE TABLE account_holders (
  account_id   BIGINT REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
  customer_id  BIGINT REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
  role         VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,  -- PRIMARY or JOINT
  PRIMARY KEY (account_id, customer_id)
);
```

**Note:** some engines allow only one NULL in a UNIQUE column; there, use a filtered unique index.

**Why it works:** a surrogate `customer_id` survives ID renewals and covers customers without a national ID, `UNIQUE` still blocks duplicate IDs, and the junction table handles joint accounts without repeating columns.

cards.title: A historical fact is not a duplicate
cards.body:
Normalisation removes copies of the **same** fact. It does not forbid recording a **different** fact that happens to look similar.

- The **tariff rate charged on a call** belongs on the call record, because it is what the customer was billed then. The tariff table holds today's rate.
- The **exchange rate applied** to a home remittance belongs on that remittance.

Ask: "If the master value changes tomorrow, should this row change too?" If no, it is a historical fact and stays.

cards.question: Business rule: every account must be domiciled at a branch that exists. Which column definition on accounts enforces this completely?
options: branch_id with a foreign key to branches, NULL allowed
branch_id NOT NULL with no foreign key
branch_id with a UNIQUE constraint
branch_id NOT NULL with a foreign key to branches
cards.explanation: The foreign key ensures any branch_id refers to a real branch, and NOT NULL ensures there always is one. A foreign key alone still accepts NULL, NOT NULL alone accepts invented IDs, and UNIQUE would allow only one account per branch.

cards.title: Tangled Archive cleared
items: A relational database stores each kind of thing in its own table, identifies rows with primary keys and links tables with foreign keys the engine enforces.
Choose a stable surrogate primary key when natural identifiers can change or be missing, and protect the natural key with a UNIQUE constraint.
One-to-many links put the foreign key on the many side; many-to-many links need a junction table with a composite key.
Update, insert and delete anomalies come from one table storing facts about several things.
1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: no dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: no dependency between non-key columns.
Use constraints and correct types (DECIMAL for money, text for identifiers) as free quality checks, and keep historical facts where they belong.

cards.prompt: Think of a spreadsheet or table your team relies on today. Which columns repeat, which facts are stored more than once, and which anomaly has already caused a real problem?

quiz.question: A customer closes her only account at Orvella Bank. Because the legacy table stores customer details only on account rows, deleting the account row also erases her address and KYC data. Which anomaly is this?
options: An update anomaly
An insert anomaly
A delete anomaly
A referential integrity violation
quiz.explanation: Losing unrelated facts (the customer's details) when you delete a row about something else (the account) is a delete anomaly. An update anomaly is inconsistent copies after a change; an insert anomaly is being unable to record a fact until another fact exists.

quiz.question: The legacy CUSTMAST table has the columns ACCOUNT1, ACCOUNT2 and ACCOUNT3. Which normal form does this design break, and what is the fix?
options: 1NF; give accounts their own table with one row per account
2NF; the account columns depend on only part of the composite key
3NF; the account columns depend on a non-key column instead of the key
None, provided unused account columns are simply left as NULL
quiz.explanation: Numbered columns for the same kind of fact are a repeating group, which breaks 1NF. The fix is a separate table with one row per account and a foreign key back to the customer. Leaving unused columns NULL does not cure the repeating group, and a fourth account still has nowhere to go.

quiz.question: Table loan_installments has key (loan_id, installment_no) and columns due_date, amount_due and borrower_name. A reviewer says the table is not in 2NF. Why?
options: due_date depends on both loan_id and installment_no, which 2NF forbids
borrower_name depends only on loan_id, part of the key
The table has a composite primary key, which 2NF does not allow
amount_due depends on due_date, which is not part of the key
quiz.explanation: 2NF requires every non-key column to depend on the whole key. The borrower is a fact about the loan, so it depends on loan_id alone: a partial dependency. Due date and amount do depend on the whole key. Composite keys are allowed; money should never be FLOAT.

quiz.question: In accounts(account_id PK, customer_id, branch_id, branch_city), the city of a branch is stored on every account. What is the correct normalisation step?
options: Add branch_city to the primary key of accounts so each pairing is unique
Split accounts into one table per city so each city's data stays together
Keep it: a single-column key means the table is already in 3NF
Move branch_city to a branches table; accounts keeps only branch_id
quiz.explanation: branch_city depends on branch_id, a non-key column, so it is a transitive dependency that breaks 3NF. It belongs in branches. A single-column key protects against 2NF problems only, not 3NF ones.

quiz.question: One Orvella branch has many accounts, and each account belongs to exactly one branch. Where should the foreign key go?
options: On branches, as an account_id column referencing accounts
In both tables, each referencing the other
On accounts, as a branch_id column referencing branches
In a junction table with branch_id and account_id
quiz.explanation: In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key goes on the many side, so each account row stores its branch_id. A column on branches could hold only one account. A junction table is for many-to-many relationships.

quiz.question: Analysts need to record that customers can hold several accounts and joint accounts can have several holders, each with a role such as PRIMARY or JOINT. Which design is correct?
options: A holder_ids column on accounts listing every holder's national ID number, separated by semicolons
A role column and an account_id column added to the customers table for each holder
Columns primary_holder_id and joint_holder_id on accounts, plus a role for each
An account_holders table (account_id, customer_id, role) keyed on the two ID columns
quiz.explanation: Many-to-many relationships need a junction table, and the role is a fact about that pairing, so it lives there too. A delimited list breaks 1NF, one account_id per customer cannot handle several accounts, and fixed holder columns are a repeating group with a hard limit.

quiz.question: Rafael plans to store wallet balances in a FLOAT column because 'it handles decimals'. Why should you object?
options: FLOAT cannot store negative values, so overdrafts and reversals would fail
FLOAT columns cannot be indexed, so balance lookups would be slow
FLOAT uses far more storage per row than DECIMAL on large tables
Floating point stores many decimals approximately, so totals drift
quiz.explanation: Floating-point types store approximations of values such as 0.10, so sums and comparisons drift and reconciliations fail. DECIMAL or NUMERIC stores exact decimal values, which is what money needs. FLOAT can be negative and can be indexed.

quiz.question: Keystone must store customers who are minors (who have no national ID card yet) and foreign nationals (who have only passports). Which primary key strategy fits best?
options: National ID number as primary key, entering zeros for customers without one
Full name plus date of birth as a composite primary key
A generated customer_id as PK, with UNIQUE on national ID where present
Mobile number as primary key, since every customer has at least one phone
quiz.explanation: A surrogate key is stable and exists for every customer, while the UNIQUE constraint still blocks duplicate national IDs and allows missing ones (in some engines via a filtered unique index). Dummy zeros would collide, names and birth dates are not reliably unique, and mobile numbers change hands.

quiz.question: Developers have been writing account status as 'A', 'Active', 'active' and 'ACT'. Reports now undercount active accounts. Which design change prevents this at the source?
options: A CHECK constraint or a foreign key to a status lookup table
A naming standard for developers, enforced through code reviews
A monthly UPDATE script that cleans the values back to one code
A wider VARCHAR column, so that every spelling fits without errors
quiz.explanation: Only a database constraint enforces allowed values for every program and user. A lookup table or CHECK stops new bad values at insert time. Standards and monthly clean-ups help but let bad data in, and a wider column makes it worse.

quiz.question: In Orvella's employees table, emp_id, national ID number and official email are each unique for every employee and none can be removed without losing uniqueness. emp_id is chosen as the primary key. What are the national ID number and official email?
options: Foreign keys, because other tables may reference them
Composite keys, because together they identify the employee
Surrogate keys, because the database checks they are unique
Candidate keys not chosen as PK (alternate keys)
quiz.explanation: Each is a minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row, so each is a candidate key. One candidate becomes the primary key and the others are alternate keys, usually protected with UNIQUE constraints. They are natural identifiers, not surrogate, foreign or composite keys.

cards.title: Numbers for the board by Friday
cards.setting: COO's office, Orvella's London branch, 14th floor. Tuesday, 4:30 pm. Rain on the windows.

lines.text: The board meets on Friday. I need three numbers: deposits by branch, active customers by city, and how many customers used instant payments last month.
I usually do this in Excel with VLOOKUPs over CSV exports. It takes two days and the totals never match Finance.
Keystone's test copy is loaded now. We'll answer all three in SQL, straight from the source, and show the query so anyone can check it.
Fine. But if the deposit total doesn't match the general ledger, the board will not trust anything else we show.
Then we write every query carefully: the right rows, the right joins, the right grouping. Ready to learn the grammar of SQL?

cards.title: The life of a SELECT statement

scenes.heading: Four families of SQL
scenes.narration: SQL has four families. DDL defines structures with CREATE, ALTER and DROP. DML works with data through SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. DCL controls access with GRANT and REVOKE. TCL controls transactions with COMMIT and ROLLBACK.

scenes.heading: Written in one order
scenes.narration: You write a query as SELECT, then FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY. That reads like English, but it is not the order the database thinks in.

scenes.heading: Processed in another
scenes.narration: Logically, the engine starts with FROM and the joins, then filters rows with WHERE, forms groups, filters groups with HAVING, and only then computes the SELECT list and sorts.

scenes.heading: Why aliases trip people up
scenes.narration: Because SELECT is worked out late, a column alias you define there does not exist yet in WHERE. You can use it in ORDER BY, which comes after.

scenes.heading: Declarative, not step by step
scenes.narration: You state what you want. The optimiser chooses how to fetch it: which index, which join method. That is why the same query can be fast one day and slow the next.

cards.title: The logical order of a query
cards.caption: When a query surprises you, walk through it in this order.

items.label: FROM and JOIN
items.detail: Pick the tables and combine their rows.

items.label: WHERE
items.detail: Keep only the rows that meet the conditions.

items.label: GROUP BY
items.detail: Collapse rows into one row per group.

items.label: HAVING
items.detail: Keep only the groups that meet conditions on aggregates.

items.label: SELECT
items.detail: Compute the output columns, aggregates and aliases.

items.label: ORDER BY
items.detail: Sort the result; aliases from SELECT can be used here.

items.label: LIMIT / TOP
items.detail: Return only the first rows, if asked. Syntax varies by engine.

cards.title: First query: big active accounts in London
cards.body:
Layla wants active accounts at London branches with balances of GBP 100,000 or more, largest first:

```sql
SELECT a.account_id,
       b.branch_name,
       a.balance
FROM   accounts a
JOIN   branches b ON b.branch_id = a.branch_id
WHERE  b.city = 'London'
  AND  a.status = 'A'
  AND  a.balance >= 100000
ORDER  BY a.balance DESC;
```

**Habits worth copying:**
- Short **table aliases** (`a`, `b`) and every column qualified, so nobody guesses which table it came from.
- Name the columns you need instead of `SELECT *`, which drags extra data and breaks when tables change.
- Text values in single quotes; numbers without.
- `IN ('A','D')` is shorthand for several ORs; `BETWEEN x AND y` **includes both ends**.
- `LIKE 'Raj%'` matches names starting with Raj; `%` is any run of characters, `_` exactly one.

cards.back: A marker for 'unknown' or 'missing'. It is not zero and not an empty string.
Never true. Any comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Use city IS NULL.
Skips rows where city is NULL as well, because NULL <> 'Dubai' is UNKNOWN, not TRUE.
COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(phone) counts only rows where phone is not NULL.
Ignores NULLs: it divides the sum of non-NULL values by how many non-NULL values there are.
Returns the first non-NULL value. Handy for labelling missing data in reports.

cards.question: Layla wants every customer who is not in Dubai, including customers whose city is missing. Which condition is correct?
options: WHERE city <> 'Dubai' OR city IS NULL
WHERE city <> 'Dubai'
WHERE city NOT IN ('Dubai', NULL)
WHERE city <> 'Dubai' AND city IS NULL
cards.explanation: city <> 'Dubai' is UNKNOWN when city is NULL, so those rows need an explicit OR city IS NULL. NOT IN with a NULL in the list is never TRUE, and the AND version can never be true for any row.

cards.title: Which join keeps which rows?
cards.caption: Most reporting uses INNER and LEFT. A RIGHT JOIN can always be rewritten as a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped.

items.label: INNER JOIN
items.right: Only customers that have at least one account

items.label: LEFT JOIN
items.right: All customers; account columns are NULL where there is none

items.label: RIGHT JOIN
items.right: All accounts, even any without a matching customer

items.label: FULL JOIN
items.right: Everything from both sides, matched where possible

items.label: CROSS JOIN
items.right: Every branch paired with every product

cards.title: LEFT JOIN, anti-joins and a classic trap
cards.body:
**Finding what is missing.** Customers who have never opened an account:

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM   customers c
LEFT JOIN account_holders h ON h.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE  h.customer_id IS NULL;
```

The LEFT JOIN keeps every customer; where there is no match, the right-hand columns are NULL, and the WHERE keeps only those. This is an **anti-join**.

**The trap.** You want every account with its instant-payment transactions, including accounts with none:

```sql
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE  t.channel = 'INSTANT'   -- silently drops accounts with no match
```

Unmatched rows have `t.channel` = NULL, so the WHERE throws them away and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an INNER JOIN. Put the condition in the **ON clause** instead: `ON t.account_id = a.account_id AND t.channel = 'INSTANT'`.

cards.title: GROUP BY, aggregates and HAVING
cards.body:
`GROUP BY` collapses rows into one row per group; aggregates (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) summarise each group.

```sql
SELECT   b.city, COUNT(*) AS accounts, SUM(a.balance) AS deposits
FROM     accounts a JOIN branches b ON b.branch_id = a.branch_id
WHERE    a.status = 'A'
GROUP BY b.city
HAVING   SUM(a.balance) > 1000000000;
```

**Rules that save you:**
- Every column in SELECT that is **not** inside an aggregate must appear in GROUP BY. Many engines reject the query otherwise; never rely on one that lets it through.
- **WHERE** filters rows before grouping; **HAVING** filters groups after. Aggregates belong in HAVING, never in WHERE.
- After a LEFT JOIN, `COUNT(*)` counts 1 for a customer with no transactions, because the row still exists. `COUNT(t.txn_id)` counts 0, because it skips NULLs.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT x)` counts different values, not rows.

cards.title: USD 1.7 billion that doesn't exist
cards.setting: MIS bay, Wednesday, 6:15 pm. Layla's first SQL report is on the big screen.

lines.text: Deposits by branch, straight from Keystone. Total: USD 4.8 billion. Finance's general ledger says 3.1 billion.
So which is wrong, the database or Finance? I can't take two numbers to the board.
Show me the query. You joined accounts to transactions to filter active accounts, then summed a.balance?
Yes. I only wanted accounts with a transaction this year.
There's the leak. The join gave one row per transaction, so every balance was repeated once for each transaction. Busy accounts were counted many times over.
Join fan-out. It's the most common way a 'correct-looking' query lies.

cards.title: Anatomy of the fan-out
cards.caption: Figures from Keystone's test copy. Always reconcile a new report to a trusted control total.

items.label: Report total
items.detail: Balances summed after joining to transactions: one row per transaction.

items.label: General ledger
items.detail: The true total of active account balances.

items.label: Phantom money
items.detail: Balances counted again for every extra transaction row.

items.label: Fix
items.detail: Filter with EXISTS or aggregate before joining.

cards.title: Stopping join fan-out
cards.body:
A join returns one row for every **matching pair**. If one account has four transactions, joining gives four rows, each repeating the balance.

| account | balance | txns | rows after join | SUM(balance) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1001 | 50,000 | 4 | 4 | 200,000 |
| 1002 | 20,000 | 1 | 1 | 20,000 |

True total: 70,000. Reported: **220,000**.

**Fixes:**
- If you only need to **filter** ("has a transaction this year"), use `EXISTS` instead of a join:

```sql
SELECT SUM(a.balance) FROM accounts a
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM transactions t
              WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id
                AND t.txn_time >= '2026-01-01');
```
- If you need figures from both tables, **aggregate each side first** to the same grain, then join.
- Check the **grain** after every join: "one row per what?"

cards.question: Account X (balance USD 10,000) has 3 transactions this month and account Y (balance USD 40,000) has 2. A query INNER JOINs accounts to this month's transactions and computes SUM(a.balance). What does it return?
cards.explanation: The join produces 3 rows for X and 2 for Y, so the sum is 10,000 x 3 + 40,000 x 2 = 110,000, not the true 50,000. Using EXISTS or pre-aggregating would avoid the fan-out.

cards.title: Real case: the spreadsheet average that skipped five countries
cards.body:
**2010:** economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff published a widely cited paper suggesting that growth slows sharply once public debt passes about 90% of GDP. It was quoted often in debates about government spending cuts.

**2013:** Thomas Herndon, a graduate student at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, tried to reproduce the results with colleagues Michael Ash and Robert Pollin. Working from the authors' own spreadsheet, they found that an averaging formula **covered only some of the rows, leaving five countries out**, and they questioned other data choices too. Reinhart and Rogoff **acknowledged the formula error**, while arguing that their main conclusions still held.

**The SQL lesson:** an aggregate over the wrong set of rows looks perfectly normal. Show **`COUNT(*)` beside every SUM or AVG**, check that the row count is the one you expect, reconcile to an independent total, and keep the query visible so others can review exactly which rows went in.

cards.title: The customers with no city
cards.situation: It is Thursday night. Layla's corrected query is ready, but 3% of active customers (about 41,000) have no city recorded, a legacy problem. Vikram wants the 'active customers by city' table in an hour and suggests: 'Just leave the blanks out, nobody will notice.' How do you handle it?

choices.text: Leave them out, as Vikram suggests. The total is only 3% lower.
choices.outcome: A board member adds up the cities and asks why the total is 41,000 short of the customer count on page two. Nobody can explain it, and confidence in every figure drops.

choices.text: Group them as 'Unknown' using COALESCE(city, 'Unknown'), so totals reconcile, and add a footnote on the data-quality fix under way.
choices.outcome: The table adds up to the true customer count, the footnote is honest, and the board asks Operations for a date to fix the missing cities. Transparent and reconcilable: the right call.

choices.text: Assign them all to Dubai, where most customers are.
choices.outcome: Dubai's number is now inflated by an invented figure. When a board member compares it with branch data, the report is exposed as manipulated. Never fill gaps with guesses.

choices.text: Refuse to produce the table until Operations has fixed every missing city.
choices.outcome: Your concern for quality is valid, but the board meeting goes ahead without the figure, and Vikram presents his own estimate. Showing missing data clearly is better than showing nothing.

cards.prompt: Rafael must mark 4,812 inactive accounts as dormant. Put the safe procedure in order.
steps: Write a SELECT with the exact WHERE clause and confirm it returns the expected 4,812 rows
Get the tested script approved and scheduled under a change ticket
Start a transaction with BEGIN
Run the UPDATE using the identical WHERE clause
Compare the rows-affected count with the SELECT count and spot-check a sample
COMMIT if everything matches; ROLLBACK if anything does not

cards.question: Layla builds a target grid with branches CROSS JOIN products. There are 12 branches and 5 products. How many rows does it return?
cards.explanation: A CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of the other: 12 x 5 = 60. It needs no join condition, which is also why an accidental cross join on large tables can explode in size.

cards.title: An UPDATE without WHERE changes everything
cards.body:
`UPDATE accounts SET status = 'D';` marks **every** account dormant. `DELETE FROM transactions;` empties the table. Both run instantly, with no warning.

- Always write and run the **SELECT** first, then swap in UPDATE or DELETE with the identical WHERE.
- Wrap changes in an explicit **transaction** so you can roll back.
- Many SQL tools have a "safe updates" setting that blocks UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE. Turn it on.
- In production, nobody should run ad hoc changes from their own login. Use approved, reviewed scripts.

cards.title: Real case: one mistyped command takes down a cloud region
cards.body:
**28 February 2017.** Amazon's S3 storage service in its US-EAST-1 region (Northern Virginia) was badly disrupted for about **four hours**, and many websites and apps that depended on it failed with it.

Amazon's published summary explained the cause. An authorised engineer was following an established procedure to take a **small number of servers** out of service. **One input to the command was entered incorrectly**, and a much larger set of servers was removed, including systems S3 needed to run. Restarting them at that scale took hours.

**What Amazon changed:** the tool now removes capacity more slowly and **refuses requests that would take a system below its safe minimum**.

**The SQL lesson:** this is the cloud version of an UPDATE without a WHERE clause. Preview the exact scope with a SELECT, compare the count with what you expect, work inside a transaction, and use tools and settings that block dangerously wide changes.

cards.title: Query Bazaar cleared
items: SQL families: DDL defines, DML reads and changes data, DCL grants access, TCL commits or rolls back.
Logical order: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. That is why WHERE cannot see SELECT aliases or aggregates.
NULL is unknown: test it with IS NULL; COUNT(col), AVG and <> comparisons skip it; COALESCE labels it.
INNER JOIN keeps matches, LEFT JOIN keeps every left row; a WHERE on the right table after a LEFT JOIN turns it into an inner join.
Every join can multiply rows. Check the grain, use EXISTS to filter, and aggregate before joining.
WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups; non-aggregated SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY.

cards.prompt: Pick a report your team produces regularly. What control total could you reconcile it to every time, and where could a join or a NULL be quietly changing the numbers?

quiz.question: A query has WHERE city = NULL and returns no rows even though many customers have no city recorded. Which change makes it work?
options: Replace it with WHERE city = ''
Replace it with WHERE city = 'NULL'
Replace it with WHERE city IS NULL
Add GROUP BY city to the query
quiz.explanation: Comparing with NULL using = yields UNKNOWN, so no rows pass. IS NULL tests for the missing marker. An empty string and the text 'NULL' are actual values, not NULL.

quiz.question: The customers table has 2,000 rows. 300 have no email address (NULL). What do COUNT(*) and COUNT(email) return?
quiz.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row, NULLs included: 2,000. COUNT(email) counts only non-NULL values: 2,000 - 300 = 1,700.

quiz.question: Layla filters txn_time BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-31' on a timestamp column and finds October totals lower than Finance's. What is the most likely cause?
options: The upper bound is 00:00 on 31 October, so that day is mostly excluded
BETWEEN excludes both end dates, so 1 and 31 October are both left out
BETWEEN only works on numeric columns and silently ignores timestamps
Timestamps must be compared with LIKE '2026-10%' to match a whole month of data
quiz.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive, but on a timestamp '2026-10-31' means 00:00 on the 31st, so transactions later that day fall outside. The safe pattern is txn_time >= '2026-10-01' AND txn_time < '2026-11-01'.

quiz.question: Vikram wants only those branches whose total instant-payment inflows exceed USD 5 million. Where does the condition on the total belong?
options: In WHERE, because every filter must run before rows are grouped
In HAVING, because it filters groups after aggregation
In ORDER BY, so the large totals appear first
In the SELECT list as an alias
quiz.explanation: Totals exist only after GROUP BY, so conditions on aggregates go in HAVING. WHERE runs before grouping and cannot use aggregates; ORDER BY sorts but does not filter.

quiz.question: This query fails: SELECT account_id, balance * 0.05 AS profit_share FROM accounts WHERE profit_share > 1000; Why?
options: Aliases cannot contain underscores in standard SQL
Arithmetic is not allowed in a SELECT list
WHERE can compare columns only with literal values, not expressions
WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet
quiz.explanation: In the logical order, WHERE comes before SELECT, so it cannot see aliases defined in SELECT. Repeat the expression (balance * 0.05 > 1000) or wrap the query in a subquery or CTE. ORDER BY, which comes after SELECT, can use the alias.

quiz.question: Compliance asks for customers who have never opened an account. Which query pattern answers this correctly?
options: customers INNER JOIN account_holders, keeping rows where account_id IS NULL
customers CROSS JOIN accounts, keeping rows where the IDs differ
customers LEFT JOIN account_holders, keeping rows where the account_holders key IS NULL
customers LEFT JOIN account_holders, keeping rows where the account_holders key IS NOT NULL
quiz.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the right side with NULL where there is no match; filtering for IS NULL keeps only the unmatched ones (an anti-join). An INNER JOIN drops those customers before the filter runs. A CROSS JOIN pairs everything with everything.

quiz.question: A report should list all accounts with a count of their instant-payment transactions, including accounts with none. The query uses accounts LEFT JOIN transactions ON account IDs, with WHERE t.channel = 'INSTANT'. Accounts without instant-payment activity are missing. What is the fix?
options: Change the LEFT JOIN to an INNER JOIN so the filter applies cleanly
Add OR t.channel IS NOT NULL to the WHERE clause
Replace COUNT with SUM in the SELECT list
Move the channel condition into the LEFT JOIN's ON clause
quiz.explanation: For unmatched accounts, t.channel is NULL, so the WHERE condition removes them and the outer join acts like an inner join. Putting the condition in ON restricts which transactions match while still keeping every account. An INNER JOIN would drop them too.

quiz.question: A branch deposit report joins accounts to transactions and sums a.balance. The total is far above the general ledger. What is the most likely cause?
options: The join repeats each balance once per transaction
The general ledger leaves out joint accounts held by two customers
SUM ignores negative balances, so overdrafts are not netted off
The report should use AVG, because SUM double-counts by design
quiz.explanation: Joining a one-row-per-account table to a many-rows-per-account table multiplies rows (fan-out), so balances are summed repeatedly. Use EXISTS to filter, or aggregate before joining. AVG would hide the problem rather than fix it.

quiz.question: Which of these statements belongs to DCL, the family that controls access?
options: CREATE TABLE branches (...)
UPDATE accounts SET status = 'D' WHERE ...
COMMIT
GRANT SELECT ON accounts TO mis_reader
quiz.explanation: GRANT and REVOKE are data control language. CREATE is DDL, UPDATE is DML and COMMIT is transaction control (TCL).

quiz.question: Keystone's database engine rejects this query: SELECT b.branch_id, b.city, SUM(a.balance) FROM accounts a JOIN branches b ON b.branch_id = a.branch_id GROUP BY b.branch_id; What is the standard fix?
options: Move SUM(a.balance) into the WHERE clause
Add b.city to the GROUP BY clause
Remove the JOIN and read city from accounts
Add HAVING b.city IS NOT NULL
quiz.explanation: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY. Adding b.city satisfies the rule and does not change the groups, because each branch has one city. Aggregates cannot go in WHERE, and HAVING does not fix the grouping rule.

cards.title: Excel gives up
cards.setting: Analytics floor, Orvella's Singapore office. Monday, 10:20 am. A spinning cursor and a frozen laptop.

lines.text: The risk committee wants the top three depositors at every branch, month-on-month deposit growth, and customers whose balance fell by half. I exported nine million rows. Excel has stopped responding.
Excel was never meant for nine million rows. And GROUP BY alone won't do it either, because you need the detail rows and the ranking together.
I'd write a loop in the app: fetch each branch, sort, keep three...
Five hundred round trips to the database? No. SQL has window functions for exactly this. One query, one pass.
Windows? Like the ones in the Window Tower on the stage map?
Exactly. You look out over a group of rows without collapsing them. Let's climb.

scenes.heading: GROUP BY squashes rows
scenes.narration: GROUP BY turns many rows into one per group. You get the branch total, but you lose the individual accounts.

scenes.heading: A window keeps every row
scenes.narration: A window function computes a value across a set of related rows, its window, and writes the answer next to each row. Nothing is collapsed.

scenes.heading: PARTITION BY sets the group
scenes.narration: PARTITION BY branch_id says: treat each branch as its own window. Rankings and totals restart at every new branch.

scenes.heading: ORDER BY sets the sequence
scenes.narration: ORDER BY inside the window decides who is first, which row is previous, and how a running total builds up.

scenes.heading: Then filter outside
scenes.narration: Window functions are calculated after WHERE, so you cannot filter on them in the same query. Compute them in a CTE or subquery, then filter in the outer query.

cards.title: Top three depositors in every branch
cards.body:
```sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT a.branch_id,
         a.account_id,
         a.balance,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY a.branch_id
                            ORDER BY a.balance DESC, a.account_id) AS rn
  FROM   accounts a
  WHERE  a.status = 'A'
)
SELECT branch_id, account_id, balance
FROM   ranked
WHERE  rn <= 3
ORDER  BY branch_id, rn;
```

**How it works:**
- The **CTE** (`WITH ranked AS ...`) is a named, temporary result that makes the query read in steps.
- `PARTITION BY branch_id` restarts numbering at each branch; `ORDER BY balance DESC` puts the largest first.
- `account_id` is a **tie-breaker**: without it, two equal balances could swap places between runs.
- The filter `rn <= 3` sits in the **outer** query, because window results do not exist yet at WHERE time.

cards.back: 1, 2, 3, 4 with no gaps and no ties. Equal values get different numbers, so add a tie-breaker to make it repeatable.
Ties share a rank and the next rank is skipped: 1, 2, 2, 4.
Ties share a rank and nothing is skipped: 1, 2, 2, 3.
The value of x from the previous or next row in the window, or NULL if there is none. Ideal for month-on-month change.
A running total: each row shows the sum of all rows up to and including it.
The group total repeated on every row, so you can show each row's share.
The whole result is one window. LAG then compares the first row of one branch with the last row of another.

cards.question: Four branches have deposits of USD 900m, 800m, 800m and 700m. What does RANK() OVER (ORDER BY deposits DESC) return, in that order?
cards.explanation: RANK gives tied values the same rank and then skips, so the branch after the tie is 4th. ROW_NUMBER would give 1, 2, 3, 4, and DENSE_RANK would give 1, 2, 2, 3.

cards.title: Subqueries, EXISTS and the NOT IN trap
cards.body:
A **subquery** is a query inside another query.
- **Scalar:** returns one value. `WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts)`.
- **List:** used with `IN`. `WHERE branch_id IN (SELECT branch_id FROM branches WHERE region = 'South')`.
- **Correlated:** refers to the outer row, so it is evaluated per row: `WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(b2.balance) FROM accounts b2 WHERE b2.branch_id = a.branch_id)`.
- **EXISTS:** true if the subquery returns any row. It can stop at the first match and does not care about NULLs.

**The NOT IN trap.** If the list contains even one NULL, `x NOT IN (list)` is never TRUE, so the query returns **no rows**:

```sql
-- returns nothing if any blocked_customers.customer_id is NULL
WHERE c.customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked_customers)
-- safe version
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked_customers b
                  WHERE b.customer_id = c.customer_id)
```

That might be my risk dashboard. It refreshes every five minutes from Keystone.
Then build the dashboards somewhere else. And Rafael says we should move OrvaPay onto a NoSQL database anyway. Is he right?
Document stores are flexible and fast. No schema to fight with.
Two separate questions. Analytics belongs in a warehouse built for it, not on the transaction system. And NoSQL is a tool for some jobs, not a replacement for a ledger.

cards.title: OLTP, OLAP and the star schema
cards.body:
| | OLTP (Keystone, OrvaPay) | OLAP (data warehouse) |
|---|---|---|
| Work | Many short reads and writes | Few large scans and aggregates |
| Design | Normalised (3NF) | Denormalised star schema |
| Data | Current state | History over years |

A **star schema** has one **fact table** at the centre and **dimension tables** around it.
- **Fact table:** one row per event at a declared **grain**, such as one row per transaction. It holds **measures** (amount, fee) and keys to dimensions.
- **Dimensions:** context for slicing: date, branch, customer, channel. They are deliberately denormalised (branch, city and region on one row) so analysts join less.
- **Slowly changing dimension type 2:** when a customer moves from the Mass to the Premier segment, add a new dimension row with `valid_from`, `valid_to` and a current flag, so old transactions still show the old segment.

Data reaches the warehouse through **ETL**: extract, transform, load.

cards.title: Real case: Netflix, a corrupted database and a move to scale-out storage
cards.body:
**August 2008.** A major database corruption left Netflix, then mainly a DVD-by-post business, **unable to ship DVDs for three days**. The company has since explained publicly that this outage pushed it away from a single large relational database in its own data centre and towards **distributed systems in the cloud** with no single point of failure. The move to the cloud took about seven years and was completed in 2016.

For huge, fast-growing data such as **viewing history**, Netflix's engineers have written about using **Apache Cassandra**, a wide-column store designed for very high write volumes spread across many servers and data centres, read back by key and time.

**The lesson:** pick the store for the workload. Wide-column stores shine for event and history data written constantly and queried by key. That does not make them the right home for every kind of data: anything that moves money still needs strict, ACID guarantees.

cards.title: Move the wallet ledger to NoSQL?
cards.situation: Rafael presents a plan: move OrvaPay's balances and transfers to a document database that replicates across data centres with eventual consistency, because 'it scales better and we can change fields without migrations'. Vikram likes the speed argument. Amara asks for your recommendation.

choices.text: Approve the full move. Flexibility and scale are what a growing wallet needs.
choices.outcome: In testing, a customer sends money twice within a second from two phones, and each replica briefly shows the old balance. Both transfers succeed and the wallet goes negative. Eventual consistency is the wrong fit for a balance that must never be overspent.

choices.text: Keep balances and transfers in the relational ledger with ACID transactions, and use a document or key-value store for flexible, non-financial data such as app preferences and session data.
choices.outcome: OrvaPay keeps strict guarantees where money moves and gains flexibility where it is harmless. The team adds a cache for read-heavy screens. This is polyglot persistence done for the right reasons.

choices.text: Reject NoSQL entirely for the bank; everything must stay relational.
choices.outcome: The ledger stays safe, but the team then forces high-volume app logs and session data into the core database, adding load where a simpler store would do. Right instinct for money, too rigid elsewhere.

choices.text: Store each wallet's full history as one JSON text column in the relational database.
choices.outcome: This gives neither benefit. The database cannot index or constrain values inside the text easily, every transfer rewrites a growing blob, and concurrent updates overwrite each other.

cards.title: Real case: the Panama Papers and the graph database
cards.body:
**2016.** The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and the German newspaper *Süddeutsche Zeitung* led the analysis of a leak of about **11.5 million documents** from Mossack Fonseca, a Panama-based law firm that set up offshore companies.

The hard question was not "how many" but **"who is connected to whom"**: companies, shareholders, directors, intermediaries and addresses, often several hops apart. ICIJ has described how it loaded these entities and links into a **graph database (Neo4j)** and gave hundreds of journalists in many countries a visual tool to explore the network. It later published much of the structure as the searchable **Offshore Leaks database**.

**The lesson:** when the questions are about **paths through relationships** (shared directors, shared addresses, shared devices), a graph model answers in one traversal what would take many self-joins in SQL. Fraud and anti-money-laundering teams use the same idea to find rings of linked accounts.

cards.title: Building a 'top N per group' query
cards.prompt: Put the steps for building the 'top three depositors per branch' query in order.
steps: Write a base SELECT of active accounts with branch_id, account_id and balance
Add ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id ORDER BY balance DESC, account_id) AS rn
Wrap that query in a CTE named ranked
Select from ranked, keeping rows where rn <= 3
Order the final output by branch_id and rn

cards.question: In June, customer Grace Wanjiru moves from the Mass segment to Premier. The warehouse must still show her March transactions under Mass. Which dimension design does this need?
options: Type 1: overwrite the segment on her existing dimension row
Store the segment only in the OLTP customers table
Type 2: insert a new customer dimension row with validity dates and point new facts to it
Delete her old facts and reload them under Premier
cards.explanation: A type 2 slowly changing dimension keeps history by adding a new row for each change, with valid_from and valid_to dates. March facts keep pointing at the Mass row. Overwriting (type 1) would rewrite history so March appears as Premier.

cards.title: Small habits for advanced SQL
cards.body:
- **UNION** removes duplicate rows, which costs a sort or hash; **UNION ALL** keeps everything and is faster. Use UNION only when you truly need duplicates removed.
- Use **CTEs** to name each step; a query that reads top to bottom is easier to review and debug.
- **CASE** turns values into categories: `CASE WHEN balance >= 1000000 THEN 'High' ELSE 'Standard' END`.
- A **correlated subquery** on millions of rows can be slow; a window function or a join to a pre-aggregated CTE often does the same in one pass.
- Always state the **grain** of your result in a comment.

cards.title: Window Tower conquered
items: Window functions add group-level values to every row: PARTITION BY sets the group, ORDER BY sets the sequence.
ROW_NUMBER gives 1,2,3,4; RANK gives 1,2,2,4; DENSE_RANK gives 1,2,2,3. Add a tie-breaker for repeatable results.
Filter window results in an outer query or CTE, because they are computed after WHERE.
Use EXISTS for 'has at least one'; prefer NOT EXISTS to NOT IN, which returns nothing if the list holds a NULL.
OLTP systems stay normalised; warehouses use star schemas, ETL and type 2 dimensions to keep history.
NoSQL families each fit specific jobs; balances that move money need ACID, not eventual consistency.

cards.prompt: Which report in your organisation still runs on the live transaction system or in a giant spreadsheet? Sketch the fact table and two dimensions a warehouse would need to answer it.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between SUM(balance) with GROUP BY branch_id and SUM(balance) OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id)?
options: The window version works only on indexed columns, so it is faster
The window version keeps every row and adds the branch total
GROUP BY returns every row with the total repeated beside it
They return exactly the same rows and values
quiz.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per branch. A window function computes the same total but leaves every input row in place, so detail and summary sit side by side.

quiz.question: Five accounts have balances of 900, 800, 800, 800 and 700 (USD thousands). What does DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY balance DESC) give the account with 700?
quiz.explanation: DENSE_RANK gives all three 800s rank 2 and continues without gaps, so 700 is rank 3. RANK would give it 5 (after three tied at 2), and ROW_NUMBER would also give 5.

quiz.question: Layla's top-three query uses ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id ORDER BY balance DESC). Two accounts at one branch have identical balances in third place, and the chosen account changes between runs. What is the best fix?
options: Add a unique tie-breaker such as account_id to the window's ORDER BY
Switch to DENSE_RANK so only one account can be third
Remove PARTITION BY so ties are compared bank-wide
Sort the outer query by balance, which makes the window order stable each run
quiz.explanation: ROW_NUMBER must give tied rows different numbers, and without a tie-breaker the order among them is arbitrary. Adding account_id makes it deterministic. DENSE_RANK would give both rank 3 and return four rows, which is a business choice, not a fix for instability.

quiz.question: Monthly deposit totals per branch sit in a CTE called monthly(branch_id, month, total). Which expression gives each month's change from the previous month for the same branch?
options: total - LEAD(total) OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id ORDER BY month)
total - SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id)
total - LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id ORDER BY month)
total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY branch_id)
quiz.explanation: LAG returns the previous row's value in the window, and partitioning by branch with ordering by month makes that the same branch's prior month. LEAD looks at the next month, SUM OVER gives the branch total, and ordering by branch alone compares unrelated rows.

quiz.question: A query computes ROW_NUMBER() ... AS rn and, in the same SELECT, uses WHERE rn <= 3. The database reports that rn is unknown. Why, and what is the fix?
options: ROW_NUMBER cannot be aliased; repeat the full expression in WHERE
Windows run after WHERE; compute rn in a CTE and filter outside
WHERE needs GROUP BY before it can use rn
Use HAVING rn <= 3 in the same query instead
quiz.explanation: Window functions run at the SELECT stage, after WHERE and HAVING, so neither can reference them. Repeating the expression in WHERE is not allowed either. Wrapping the ranking in a CTE makes rn an ordinary column for the outer filter.

quiz.question: Which statement about the subquery in WHERE a.balance > (SELECT AVG(b.balance) FROM accounts b WHERE b.branch_id = a.branch_id) is true?
options: It is correlated: it depends on the outer row's branch_id
It is a scalar subquery that runs exactly once for the whole query
It is invalid, because a subquery cannot refer to an outer table
It returns a list, so it must be used with IN
quiz.explanation: The inner query uses a.branch_id from the outer query, which makes it correlated: conceptually it is evaluated per outer row, comparing each account to its own branch average. It returns one value, but a different one per branch, so it is not a single run.

quiz.question: A sanctions-screening query uses WHERE c.customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM watchlist_matches). After an import, it returns no customers at all, although most are clearly not on the list. What happened?
options: A row with a NULL customer_id was imported, and NOT IN fails against NULL
The watchlist became too large for NOT IN to process
NOT IN only works when both columns are indexed
The import changed the data type of customer_id, so no values compare as equal
quiz.explanation: If any value in the list is NULL, x NOT IN (list) evaluates to UNKNOWN for every x that is not found, so no row passes. NOT EXISTS, or filtering NULLs out of the subquery, avoids this.

quiz.question: A telco's fraud team wants to find groups of SIMs, devices and wallet accounts linked through shared handsets and shared ID numbers, several hops apart. Which NoSQL family fits this analysis best?
options: A key-value store
A wide-column store
A document store
A graph database
quiz.explanation: Graph databases store nodes and relationships directly and make multi-hop traversals natural, which suits fraud rings. Key-value stores give fast single-key lookups, wide-column stores handle high-volume time series, and document stores hold flexible records.

quiz.question: Layla's risk dashboard runs heavy aggregation queries every five minutes against Keystone's live database, slowing down wallet payments. What is the best long-term design?
options: Feed a separate data warehouse via ETL and point the dashboard there
Add more indexes to every Keystone table so the dashboard queries run faster
Refresh the dashboard every minute so each query is smaller
Run the dashboard queries with READ UNCOMMITTED on Keystone
quiz.explanation: Transaction systems (OLTP) and analytics (OLAP) have different workloads. Moving analytics to a warehouse protects payment performance and allows a star schema built for reporting. Extra indexes slow writes, and dirty reads give wrong numbers.

quiz.question: In a warehouse star schema for wallet payments, which item belongs in the fact table?
options: The customer's segment and city
The month name and fiscal quarter
The payment amount, with keys to its dimensions
The channel description, such as USSD, app or agent
quiz.explanation: Fact tables hold measures at the declared grain plus foreign keys to dimensions. Descriptive attributes such as segment, city, month names and channel descriptions belong in dimension tables, where they are used to slice and filter facts.

sessions.title: Performance and Concurrency: Indexes, Plans, Transactions and Locks
sessions.summary: Salary day exposes slow queries and a double debit. Learn how indexes and execution plans work, how to write index-friendly SQL, and how ACID transactions, isolation levels and locks keep money safe when thousands of users act at once.
objectives: Explain B-tree indexes, clustered and non-clustered indexes and their costs
Design composite and covering indexes and write sargable predicates
Read an execution plan and spot scans, lookups and stale statistics
Explain ACID, isolation levels and the dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom and lost update problems
Prevent double debits and deadlocks with atomic updates, locking order, short transactions and idempotency keys

cards.title: Salary day, 9:02 am
cards.setting: Operations war room, Orvella's Nairobi office. Salary day, the last working day of the month.

lines.text: Salaries for 1.3 million customers landed at 9:00. By 9:02 the war room's screens have turned red.
The OrvaPay mini-statement screen takes forty seconds. Customers are posting screenshots on social media and the call centre queue is at 6,000.
The statement query hasn't changed in months. It was fine in testing!
Testing had fifty thousand transactions. Production now has 900 million. Pull the execution plan for that query.
It says... table scan on transactions. Rows read: 900 million. To return the last ten transactions for one wallet.
Then the database is reading the whole library to find one page. Today you learn how indexes work, and how to read a plan.

cards.title: How an index finds one row in a billion

scenes.heading: The unsorted ledger
scenes.narration: Without an index, the database must read every row of the table to find the ones you asked for. That is a full table scan, and it grows with the table.

scenes.heading: A sorted tree of keys
scenes.narration: An index keeps a copy of chosen columns in sorted order, usually in a balanced tree called a B-tree, with pointers back to the full rows.

scenes.heading: Seek, don't scan
scenes.narration: To find wallet 7731, the engine walks down the tree in a handful of steps and lands on exactly the right entries. That is an index seek.

scenes.heading: The optimiser decides
scenes.narration: The query optimiser estimates how many rows each option will touch, using statistics about the data, and picks the cheapest plan. The execution plan shows its choice.

scenes.heading: Nothing is free
scenes.narration: Every index must be updated on every insert, update and delete, and it takes disk space. Good indexes are chosen for real queries, not added everywhere.

cards.title: Clustered or non-clustered index?
cards.caption: Terms and defaults vary by engine; some engines store tables as unordered heaps unless told otherwise.

items.label: What it stores
items.left: The table rows themselves, in key order
items.right: A sorted copy of key columns plus a row pointer

items.label: How many per table
items.left: One, because rows can be sorted only one way
items.right: Many

items.label: Typical key
items.left: The primary key, often an ever-increasing ID
items.right: Columns you filter or join on

items.label: After a match
items.right: May need a lookup into the table for other columns

cards.title: Composite and covering indexes
cards.body:
OrvaPay's statement query:

```sql
SELECT txn_time, amount, channel
FROM   transactions
WHERE  wallet_id = 7731
ORDER  BY txn_time DESC
LIMIT  10;
```

**Composite index:** one index on several columns, sorted by the first, then the second:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ix_txn_wallet_time ON transactions (wallet_id, txn_time);
```

- It serves `wallet_id = ?` and `wallet_id = ? AND txn_time >= ?`, and already returns rows in time order.
- It generally does **not** help a filter on `txn_time` alone: like a phone book sorted by surname then first name, you cannot search by first name. This is the **leftmost-prefix rule**.
- Put **equality** columns first, then the **range** or sort column.

**Covering index:** if the index also holds `amount` and `channel` (for example with `INCLUDE`, where supported), the query is answered from the index alone, with no lookups into the table.

cards.question: Keystone has an index on transactions (wallet_id, txn_time). Which query can use it for an efficient seek?
options: WHERE txn_time >= '2026-11-01'
WHERE wallet_id = 7731 AND txn_time >= '2026-11-01'
WHERE amount > 50000
WHERE channel = 'INSTANT'
cards.explanation: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then its second, so a seek needs the leading column. A filter on txn_time alone, amount or channel cannot use the sort order efficiently in most engines.

cards.title: Index-friendly or index-blocking?
cards.prompt: Each WHERE clause runs against a column that has a normal B-tree index. Sort them by whether the index can be used for a seek.

items.text: national_id = 880312456789 when national_id is a text column

cards.title: Write predicates the index can use
cards.body:
A condition is **sargable** (search-argument-able) when the engine can compare the raw column against a value and seek into the index.

**Index killers:**
- **Functions on the column:** `YEAR(txn_time) = 2026`. Rewrite as a range.
- **Arithmetic on the column:** `amount * 1.17 > 10000`. Move the maths to the other side.
- **Leading wildcard:** `LIKE '%4567'` cannot use a B-tree sorted from the first character. Store a searchable column, such as the last four digits, or use a dedicated search feature.
- **Implicit conversion:** comparing a text `national_id` column with a number makes the engine convert every row. Compare like with like: `national_id = '880312456789'`.

**Reading the plan:** run `EXPLAIN` (or your tool's 'show plan'). Look for **scans** on big tables, **lookups** repeated thousands of times, and a big gap between **estimated and actual rows**, which usually means **stale statistics**. Refresh them and re-check.

cards.title: The fix, measured
cards.caption: Keystone test results. One well-designed index beat any amount of extra hardware.

items.label: Before
items.detail: Full scan of the transactions table for every statement request.

items.label: Rows read before
items.detail: Every transaction ever made, to return ten.

items.label: After
items.detail: Seek on (wallet_id, txn_time) with amount and channel included.

items.label: Rows read after
items.detail: Just the ten newest entries for that wallet.

cards.title: Choosing indexes like a professional
cards.body:
- Index for **real, frequent queries**, starting from the execution plan, not from a guess.
- Columns with few distinct values (a gender flag, a three-value status) rarely help on their own: the engine would still read a large share of the table, so it often prefers a scan.
- Every extra index slows **INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE** and uses storage. On a busy transaction table, five good indexes beat twenty overlapping ones.
- Check index **usage statistics** regularly and drop indexes nothing uses.
- Test with **production-like volumes**: a query that is fast on 50,000 rows can collapse at 900 million.

cards.title: Charged twice for one bill
cards.setting: OrvaPay support desk, salary day, 2:30 pm. Mei forwards a complaint.

lines.text: Mr Samuel Otieno in Kisumu paid his electricity bill of KES 2,500 once. OrvaPay debited him twice, and his wallet now shows minus KES 1,300.
Impossible. The code checks the balance before debiting.
Show me the code. You read the balance, check it in the app, then write balance minus 2,500?
Yes. And his phone retried the request when the network dropped, so two requests arrived 40 milliseconds apart.
Then both requests read 3,700, both passed the check, and both wrote. Two transactions interleaved, and the database did exactly what it was told.
How many other customers did this happen to today? And how do we make it impossible?

cards.back: All or nothing. A transfer's debit and credit both happen, or neither does.
A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another; every constraint still holds afterwards.
Concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work. Isolation levels set how strict this is.
Once committed, a change survives a crash or power cut, because it was first written to the transaction log.
Makes the transaction's changes permanent and visible to others.
Undoes everything the transaction did since it began.

cards.title: Isolation levels and what they prevent
cards.caption: Stricter levels mean more locking or more aborted transactions. Defaults vary: several engines default to read committed, others to repeatable read.

items.label: Read uncommitted
items.right: Nothing: dirty reads of uncommitted data are possible

items.label: Read committed
items.right: Dirty reads

items.label: Repeatable read
items.right: Dirty and non-repeatable reads; phantoms possible in the standard

items.label: Serializable
items.right: All three: the result is as if transactions ran one at a time

cards.title: Four concurrency problems
cards.body:
- **Dirty read:** you read a change another transaction has not committed; it rolls back, and you acted on data that never existed.
- **Non-repeatable read:** you read a row twice in one transaction and get different values, because someone committed an update in between.
- **Phantom read:** you run the same range query twice and **new rows** appear (or disappear) because someone inserted or deleted.
- **Lost update:** two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value, and the second write overwrites the first.
- **Check-then-act race:** both check the same old balance, then both debits apply. That is Mr Otieno's case.

**Locks:** a **shared (S)** lock lets others read but not write; an **exclusive (X)** lock blocks everyone else. Many readers can share; writers wait.

**MVCC:** many engines keep row versions, so readers see a consistent **snapshot** without blocking writers. Snapshot-based levels are useful for long reports on busy systems.

cards.question: Inside one transaction, a loan check reads Mr Otieno's wallet balance twice. Between the two reads, a bill payment commits and the second read shows a lower balance. Which problem is this?
options: A dirty read
A phantom read
A deadlock
A non-repeatable read
cards.explanation: The same row returned a different value within one transaction because another transaction committed an update in between: a non-repeatable read. It is not dirty, because the change was committed, and not a phantom, which is about rows appearing in a range.

cards.title: Real case: the bitcoin bank emptied by a race condition
cards.body:
**March 2014.** Flexcoin, a small bitcoin bank, announced that it was **closing down** after an attacker stole **896 bitcoins**, worth roughly **USD 600,000** at the time.

According to the company's own statement, the attacker exploited a flaw in the code that moved coins **between Flexcoin users**. By firing many transfer requests at the same instant, the attacker got several of them to pass the balance check **before any of them had updated the balance**. Coins were effectively created out of thin air and then withdrawn.

That is exactly the **check-then-act race** in Mr Otieno's double debit: read the balance, decide in the application, then write. Under concurrency, every request can see the same old balance.

**The lesson:** make the check and the change **one atomic step** in the database (a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount`, or a row lock), and test money-moving code with many simultaneous requests, not one at a time.
