cards.title: Making the double debit impossible
cards.situation: Amara asks you to fix OrvaPay's bill payment so Mr Otieno's case can never repeat. The current code reads the balance, checks it in the app, then writes balance minus amount. Phones sometimes resend a request when the network drops. Which design do you recommend?

choices.text: Check and debit in one atomic statement, UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 2500 WHERE wallet_id = ? AND balance >= 2500, and store each request ID under a UNIQUE constraint.
choices.outcome: Concurrent requests now queue on the row lock, and the second one finds the balance too low or its request ID already used. No double debits, no overdrawn wallets, and normal traffic stays fast. This is the robust fix.

choices.text: Set the whole database to serializable isolation so all transactions run as if one at a time.
choices.outcome: The double debit stops, but throughput drops sharply on salary day and many transactions are aborted and must be retried. It treats the symptom with a sledgehammer, and a resent request with a new transaction can still be processed twice.

choices.text: Add a 500-millisecond pause in the app before each debit so requests do not overlap.
choices.outcome: Requests still overlap under load; the pause just makes every payment slower. Timing tricks never fix race conditions.

choices.text: Leave the code and run a nightly reconciliation to refund double debits.
choices.outcome: Customers are overdrawn for a day, complaints keep coming, and reconciliation itself becomes a risk. Detecting errors is useful, but it must not replace preventing them.

cards.title: Concurrency vocabulary
cards.prompt: Match each term to what it means in Keystone.

pairs.right: Held while reading; other readers may also hold it, but writers must wait
Held while writing; blocks other readers that need locks and all other writers
Reads a row and locks it so nobody else can change it before you write
Checks a version number at write time and fails if someone else changed the row first
Two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds, so neither can continue
A unique request ID that ensures a resent request is processed only once

cards.title: The 3 am deadlock alert
cards.body:
Two OrvaPay transfers run at the same moment:

| Time | Transaction 1 (Sofia to Arjun) | Transaction 2 (Arjun to Sofia) |
|---|---|---|
| t1 | locks Sofia's wallet | locks Arjun's wallet |
| t2 | waits for Arjun's wallet | waits for Sofia's wallet |

Neither can move. The database detects the **deadlock**, picks one transaction as the **victim**, rolls it back and returns an error; the other completes.

**What the team changed:**
- **Lock in a consistent order:** always update the wallet with the lower `wallet_id` first, whoever is sending.
- **Keep transactions short:** no network calls, OTP prompts or user input while locks are held.
- **Retry the victim** automatically, a limited number of times, with the same idempotency key.
- **Index the lookup columns**, so the database locks only the rows it needs.

cards.title: Investigating a slow query
cards.prompt: Put Amara's routine for a slow query in order.
steps: Capture the exact query text and the parameter values that were slow
Get the execution plan with actual row counts
Read the plan for scans, repeated lookups and gaps between estimated and actual rows
Design a fix (rewrite, index or refreshed statistics) and test it on production-like volumes
Deploy the fix through change control
Monitor response times afterwards and compare them with the old baseline

cards.question: Two report sessions hold shared locks on Mr Otieno's wallet row. A third session wants to read it, and a fourth wants to update it. What happens?
options: The reader gets a shared lock at once; the updater waits for an exclusive lock
Both get their locks at once
Both must wait until the reports finish
The updater goes first, because writes have priority
cards.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with each other, so another reader can join. An exclusive lock is incompatible with any other lock, so the writer waits until the shared locks are released.

cards.title: Real case: TSB's 2018 platform migration
cards.body:
**April 2018.** UK bank TSB moved its customers' records from its former parent's systems to a new banking platform over one weekend. When it switched on, **many customers could not log in, saw wrong information or could not make payments**, and problems lasted for weeks.

- An independent review for TSB's board, published in **2019**, concluded that the new platform **was not ready** to go live and that **testing had not given enough assurance** that it would cope in real use.
- In **December 2022**, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority and Prudential Regulation Authority **fined TSB about GBP 49 million** in total for failings in how it managed the operational risk of the migration. TSB had already paid compensation to affected customers.

**The lesson:** a system that works in testing can still fail at go-live if it was not proven with **production-like volumes, real traffic patterns and a tested fallback**. Performance is not a feature you add after launch.

cards.title: Salary-Day Storm survived
items: Indexes are sorted structures (usually B-trees) that turn scans into seeks; they speed reads but slow writes and use space.
A composite index serves filters on its leading columns: equality columns first, then range or sort columns. A covering index avoids table lookups.
Functions, arithmetic or conversions on a column, and leading wildcards, block index seeks. Read the plan and compare estimated with actual rows.
ACID: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable. Isolation levels trade safety against concurrency; know your engine's default.
Prevent lost updates with atomic conditional updates or row locks, and duplicate requests with idempotency keys.
Avoid deadlocks with a consistent lock order and short transactions, and retry the victim.

cards.prompt: Think about the busiest moment in your organisation's month. Which query or transaction would fail first under that load, and what would its execution plan reveal?

quiz.question: Rafael proposes adding an index on every column of the transactions table 'so all queries are fast'. What is the main drawback?
options: Every write must also update every index, and indexes use storage
Indexes make SELECT queries return rows in a random, unpredictable order
A table can have only one index
Indexes stop the database from enforcing foreign keys
quiz.explanation: Indexes speed suitable reads but must be maintained on every write and take space, which hurts a busy transaction table. Tables can have many non-clustered indexes, and indexes do not affect constraint enforcement.

quiz.question: An index exists on transactions (account_id, txn_time). Which query is least likely to use it for a seek?
options: WHERE account_id = 5501
WHERE txn_time >= '2026-11-01' AND txn_time < '2026-11-02'
WHERE account_id = 5501 AND txn_time BETWEEN '2026-11-01' AND '2026-11-02'
WHERE account_id = 5501 ORDER BY txn_time DESC
quiz.explanation: Composite indexes are sorted by the leading column first, so a filter on txn_time alone cannot seek in most engines (the leftmost-prefix rule). All the other queries filter on account_id, and the last also benefits from the index's time order.

quiz.question: Which rewrite of WHERE YEAR(txn_time) = 2026 lets an index on txn_time be used for a seek?
options: WHERE CAST(txn_time AS DATE) BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
WHERE YEAR(txn_time) >= 2026 AND YEAR(txn_time) <= 2026
WHERE txn_time >= '2026-01-01' AND txn_time < '2027-01-01'
WHERE txn_time LIKE '2026%'
quiz.explanation: Wrapping the column in a function or conversion stops a seek, so the safe form compares the raw column with a half-open range. The CAST, YEAR and LIKE versions all transform the column, and LIKE on a timestamp also forces a conversion.

quiz.question: Why can a table have only one clustered index?
options: The SQL standard forbids a table from having more than one index of any kind
It stores the rows themselves in key order, and rows sort only one way
Because clustered indexes are only allowed on primary keys
Because a clustered index copies the whole table into memory
quiz.explanation: A clustered index defines how the table's rows are stored, so there can be only one. Non-clustered indexes are separate sorted copies of some columns, and a table can have many. A clustered key is often, but not necessarily, the primary key.

quiz.question: An OrvaPay transfer debits Hana's wallet and credits Omar's. The server crashes after the debit but before the credit. Which ACID property ensures Hana does not lose the money?
options: Durability
Atomicity
Isolation
Consistency
quiz.explanation: Atomicity means the transaction's changes happen all together or not at all, so the uncommitted debit is rolled back during recovery. Durability protects committed changes, and isolation concerns concurrent transactions.

quiz.question: The database confirms a commit for an instant-payment credit, and a second later the power fails. On restart the credit is still there. Which mechanism makes this possible?
options: The app kept the change in memory and resent it once the server restarted
The database confirms commits only after the nightly backup
Isolation prevented the power failure from affecting it
The change reached the transaction log before the commit was confirmed
quiz.explanation: Durability is achieved by writing changes to the transaction log on stable storage before acknowledging the commit. On restart, recovery uses the log to restore committed work and undo uncommitted work.

quiz.question: An analyst's report shows a branch balance that includes a large deposit that was later rolled back by the teller system. Under which isolation level was the report most likely running?
options: Read committed
Repeatable read
Read uncommitted
Serializable
quiz.explanation: Seeing uncommitted changes that are then rolled back is a dirty read, which only read uncommitted allows. Read committed and stricter levels show only committed data.

quiz.question: Two requests to debit the same wallet arrive together. Each reads balance 3,700, checks that 2,500 is available, and writes 1,200. Which change prevents this lost update without slowing the whole system?
options: Read the balance a second time just before writing, to confirm that it has not changed
Run all wallet transactions under read uncommitted
UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 2500 WHERE wallet_id = ? AND balance >= 2500
Cache balances in the app for faster checks
quiz.explanation: The atomic conditional update reads and writes under one row lock, so the second request sees the updated balance and fails the condition. Reading twice does not stop interleaving, read uncommitted makes things worse, and a cache adds stale data.

quiz.question: The database reports that an OrvaPay transfer was chosen as a deadlock victim. What has happened, and what should the application do?
options: It was committed twice; the app should reverse one of the two copies
The database crashed; the app should wait for a restart
It was rolled back to break the deadlock; the app should retry it
The transaction is still waiting; the app should cancel the other one
quiz.explanation: When two transactions wait on each other, the database picks a victim, rolls it back and returns an error so the other can finish. The application should retry the victim a limited number of times, using an idempotency key so the retry cannot double-process.

quiz.question: A table of 20 million customers has an index on gender, which has two values. Queries filtering on gender still use a full scan. Why?
options: Indexes cannot be created on text columns such as gender in most engines
The index must be rebuilt every time a query runs
The optimiser never uses indexes on tables over 10 million rows
Low selectivity: each value matches half the table, so a scan is cheaper
quiz.explanation: An index helps when it narrows the search to a small share of rows. With two values, each matches millions of rows, and many separate lookups cost more than one sequential scan, so the optimiser rightly ignores the index.

sessions.title: Protecting the Data: Backup, Recovery, Security and Privacy
sessions.summary: A storage failure and an injection attack hit on the same night. Plan backup and recovery around RPO and RTO, build a restore chain, close the door on SQL injection with least privilege, encryption and masking, and apply the data-protection principles shared by laws around the world.
objectives: Define RPO and RTO and design a backup schedule that meets them
Build a correct restore chain with full, differential, log and tail-log backups and recover to a point in time
Explain why replicas and snapshots are not backups and how to protect backups from ransomware
Prevent SQL injection and apply least privilege, encryption, hashing, masking and auditing
Apply the core principles shared by data-protection laws worldwide and check the rules where the data is held and used

cards.title: 2:40 am, six days before go-live
cards.setting: Your phone buzzes in the dark. A WhatsApp call from Amara.

lines.text: Sorry to wake you. A storage controller failed at 2:10 and corrupted Keystone's data files. The database won't start. I need you on the bridge call now.
By 2:55 the bridge call is full: Amara, Rafael, Mei, and Vikram, who sounds as if he has not slept at all.
Go-live is in six days. How much data have we lost, and when is it back?
That depends on two numbers we agreed with the business months ago, and on whether our backups actually restore.
And one more thing. While you were all asleep, our logs show someone typing ' OR '1'='1 into the OrvaPay complaint form. Hundreds of times.
Recovery first, security second, but tonight we deal with both. This is the final stage.

cards.title: Backups, logs and the road back

scenes.heading: Full backup
scenes.narration: A full backup copies the whole database at a moment in time. It is the foundation every restore starts from.

scenes.heading: Differential and incremental
scenes.narration: A differential copies everything changed since the last full backup, so you only ever need the latest one. An incremental copies changes since the last backup of any kind, so you need every one in the chain.

scenes.heading: Transaction log backups
scenes.narration: Log backups capture every committed change since the previous log backup. Taken every few minutes, they let you replay history almost to the second.

scenes.heading: Point-in-time recovery
scenes.narration: Restore the full backup, the latest differential, then the logs in sequence, and stop exactly where you choose: for example, one second before someone ran a bad DELETE.

scenes.heading: A backup is a promise until tested
scenes.narration: Untested backups fail when you need them most. Only a regular, timed test restore proves the backup works and shows how long recovery really takes.

cards.title: Keystone's agreed recovery targets
cards.caption: RPO drives how often you back up; RTO drives how fast you must be able to restore. Both are business decisions.

items.label: RPO
items.detail: Recovery point objective: the most data, measured in time, the business accepts losing.

items.label: RTO
items.detail: Recovery time objective: the longest the service may be down before it is restored.

items.label: Log backups
items.detail: Taken every 15 minutes and copied off the server, to support the RPO.

items.label: Copies
items.detail: At least three copies, on two kinds of media, one off site.

cards.question: Keystone takes transaction log backups every 15 minutes. The disk holding both data and log fails at 10:52, and the most recent log backup finished at 10:45. If nothing more can be saved, how much committed data is lost?
options: About 15 minutes: the full backup interval
About 7 minutes: everything committed after 10:45
Nothing, because the log is replayed automatically
Everything since the last full backup
cards.explanation: The restore can reach the end of the 10:45 log backup, so transactions from 10:45 to 10:52 are lost: about 7 minutes, within the 15-minute RPO. If the log disk had survived, a tail-log backup could have saved those minutes too.

cards.title: Building the restore chain
cards.body:
Keystone's schedule: **full** every Sunday 23:00, **differential** every night at 23:00, **log** backups every 15 minutes.

To recover from a failure on Thursday morning:
1. **Tail-log backup:** if the log file survived, back up its final part first, so nothing since the last log backup is lost.
2. Restore **Sunday's full** backup, without bringing the database online yet.
3. Restore **Wednesday night's differential** only. Differentials are cumulative, so Monday's and Tuesday's are not needed.
4. Apply **every log backup taken after that differential**, in order, then the tail-log. A missing log file breaks the chain.
5. **Recover** and open the database, then run integrity checks and reconcile key totals.

**Point in time:** if the problem is a mistaken `DELETE` at 14:07:30, replay the logs and **stop at 14:07:29**. Restoring only the last full backup would lose a whole day.

**Restore time counts against the RTO.** Measure it in drills, not on the night.

cards.title: The 3 am restore
cards.prompt: Put the team's recovery steps in order.
steps: Declare the incident and stop applications writing to the damaged database
Take a tail-log backup if the log is still readable
Restore the latest full backup without recovering the database
Restore the latest differential backup
Apply every later log backup in sequence, then the tail-log
Recover the database, run integrity checks and reconcile totals
Reopen to users and record the actual data loss and downtime

cards.title: Real backup or false comfort?
cards.prompt: Rafael lists everything that 'protects' Keystone's data. Which items give real recovery protection on their own?
buckets: Not a backup on its own

items.text: Nightly full and 15-minute log backups copied to immutable storage in another city
A synchronous replica in the same data centre
RAID 10 on the database server's disks
Weekly encrypted backups on tape kept off site, with restore tests
Storage snapshots kept on the same array as the database
A disaster-recovery standby that replicates every change within seconds
Monthly Excel exports of the main tables
Full and log backups copied to a separate backup server under different admin credentials

cards.title: Replication is not backup
cards.body:
Replicas, standbys and RAID protect against **hardware failure**. They faithfully copy whatever happens, including a mistaken `DELETE`, corrupted data or ransomware encryption, within seconds.

- Keep backups **separate**: different storage, ideally a different site, and **different credentials** from production admins.
- Keep at least one copy **immutable or offline**, so an attacker who controls the servers cannot delete it.
- **Encrypt** backups, and store the keys away from the backups themselves.
- Run a **timed test restore** regularly and compare it with the RTO.

cards.title: Real case: GitLab's six lost hours
cards.body:
**31 January 2017.** While fighting a production problem late at night, an engineer at GitLab, the code-hosting company, ran a command to clear a database directory, intending it for the **secondary** server. It ran on the **primary**. Around **300 GB** of live data was gone in seconds.

Then the team discovered, as they reported publicly, that **several of their backup methods had not been working**: scheduled database dumps had been failing silently, and the failure alerts were not getting through. The best surviving copy was a snapshot taken about **six hours earlier** for a test environment.

GitLab restored from it and **lost roughly six hours of database changes** (issues, merge requests, comments and new accounts), though the code in users' Git repositories was not affected. It published a frank post-mortem and fixed its backup monitoring.

**The lesson:** a backup nobody has restored is only a hope. Monitor every backup job, alert on failure, and prove recovery with regular, timed test restores.

cards.title: ' OR '1'='1
cards.setting: Bridge call, 3:30 am. Keystone is restoring. Mei shares her screen.

lines.text: The complaint form's tracking search builds its SQL like this: "SELECT * FROM complaints WHERE ref = '" + userInput + "'". Someone typed ' OR '1'='1 and got every complaint back.
That form was a quick fix two years ago... I'm sorry.
It gets worse. The form connects to the database as a database owner account. With the right input, an attacker could have read customer tables or dropped them.
Did they get customer data?
The audit log suggests they only reached complaints. But only because they didn't try harder.
Two failures, then: code that mixes data with commands, and an account with far more power than it needs. Both are fixable before go-live.

cards.title: SQL injection and the real fix
cards.body:
**Injection** happens when user input is pasted into SQL text, so the input can change the command itself. The input `' OR '1'='1` turns the filter into one that is always true.

**The fix is parameterised queries** (prepared statements). The SQL text is fixed, and input travels separately as data:

```sql
SELECT ref, status FROM complaints WHERE ref = ?;   -- input bound to ?
```

The database never treats the bound value as code, whatever characters it contains.

**Watch out:**
- A **stored procedure** that concatenates input into dynamic SQL is still injectable. Parameterise the dynamic SQL too.
- **Escaping quotes** by hand and **blocklists** are fragile; treat **input validation** (expected length, format) as an extra layer, not the fix.
- **Least privilege** limits the damage if something slips through: a form that can only read one view cannot drop tables.
- Never show raw database errors to users; they help attackers map the schema.

cards.title: Control for the threat
cards.prompt: Mei's go-live checklist. Match each control to the threat it addresses most directly.

pairs.right: Attacker types SQL fragments into a search box
A compromised reporting login tries to read and change every table
Someone captures traffic between the app servers and the database
A disk or backup file is stolen and opened on another server
Call-centre agents see full national ID numbers and balances they do not need
An insider quietly browses a celebrity customer's account

cards.title: Real case: TalkTalk and the forgotten web pages

cards.question: The OrvaPay complaint form needs to look up the status of one complaint by reference number. What database access should its account have?
options: Database owner, so the form never hits permission errors
SELECT on all tables, since it only reads
EXECUTE on a single lookup procedure (or SELECT on one narrow view), and nothing else
The same shared login the developers use, to simplify support
cards.explanation: Least privilege grants only what the function needs, so a flaw in the form exposes as little as possible. Read access to all tables still exposes every customer record, and shared logins destroy accountability.

cards.title: A copy of production for testing
cards.situation: The Keystone vendor's testers in Kuala Lumpur ask for a full copy of the production database in the test environment 'to find edge cases before go-live'. It holds 3.2 million customers' names, national ID numbers, phone numbers and balances. Vikram says yes, because time is short. Mei asks what you recommend.

choices.text: Copy it as is. Testers are under a contract and testing with real data finds the most bugs.
choices.outcome: The test environment has weaker controls and wider access. Months later, a tester's laptop with an extract is lost, and real customers' data is exposed. Contracts do not make an unprotected copy safe.

choices.text: Copy it, but restrict the test database to five named testers.
choices.outcome: Fewer people see it, which helps, but real identities and balances still sit in a less protected environment and in testers' extracts. Risk is reduced, not removed.

choices.text: Create the copy through an approved process that statically masks or pseudonymises personal fields before the data leaves production, keeps keys and formats consistent so tests still work, and logs who receives it.
choices.outcome: Testers get realistic volumes and edge cases, ID number formats and relationships still hold, and no real customer can be identified. Mei signs off and the copy becomes a reusable, controlled process. This is the professional answer.

choices.text: Refuse and tell testers to type in 50 sample customers by hand.
choices.outcome: Nothing leaks, but the tiny dataset misses the volume and messy edge cases that cause real failures, as salary day showed. Safe, but it weakens the testing you need.

cards.title: Protecting data at rest and on screen

cards.back: TLS between app and database, so captured traffic cannot be read.
Encrypts data files and backups on disk. Authorised queries still see plain data, so it does not stop a misused login.
Encrypts specific sensitive columns; only holders of the key can read them, even inside the database.
Store a salted hash from a slow algorithm built for passwords, never the password itself or a fast unsalted hash.
Permanently replaces real values in a copy, such as for testing. The original never leaves production.
Hides values at query time by role: an agent sees XXX-XXX-4821 while the data stays intact.
Swaps a sensitive value for a meaningless token; the real value is kept in a separate, tightly controlled vault.

cards.title: Data protection around the world
cards.caption: A map, not legal advice. Laws are amended and new ones arrive often: confirm the current rules with your compliance and legal teams.

items.label: OECD Privacy Guidelines
items.detail: First international statement of core principles such as purpose limitation, data quality and security safeguards. Updated in 2013.

items.label: Council of Europe Convention 108
items.detail: The first binding international treaty on personal data, open to countries outside Europe too.

items.label: Singapore PDPA
items.detail: Personal Data Protection Act covering private-sector organisations, with a national regulator.

items.label: EU GDPR
items.detail: Adopted in 2016 and applied from May 2018. The most widely copied model. Fines can reach EUR 20m or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

items.label: Kenya Data Protection Act
items.detail: Brought GDPR-style principles, data subject rights and a Data Protection Commissioner to Kenya.

items.label: India DPDP Act
items.detail: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, built around consent, purpose and a Data Protection Board.

items.label: Your job today
items.detail: Check what applies where you work. Pakistan, for example, relies on PECA 2016 and regulator rules while a dedicated law is debated.

cards.title: Personal data: principles that travel
cards.body:
Laws differ in detail, but most, from the EU's **GDPR** to Singapore's **PDPA**, Kenya's **Data Protection Act** and India's **DPDP Act**, share principles that go back to the OECD Guidelines:
- **Purpose limitation:** collect data for a defined, legitimate purpose and do not reuse it for something unrelated.
- **Minimisation:** hold only what that purpose needs.
- **Retention:** keep records as long as the purpose or the law requires (for example, financial record-keeping rules), then delete or anonymise.
- **Security and need-to-know access,** logged and reviewed.
- **Transfers:** many laws restrict sending personal data abroad without safeguards, and banking regulators often add outsourcing and cloud rules or approvals.
- **Breach readiness:** under the GDPR, a reportable breach must normally reach the regulator within 72 hours; other laws set their own timelines.

**Check the rules where you work.** Sector regulators for banking, telecoms and health add duties on top of the general law.

cards.question: Rafael's code fixes the complaint search by moving the concatenated SQL into a stored procedure that builds a query string from @ref and executes it. Is the injection fixed?
options: No: dynamic SQL built by concatenating @ref is still injectable; the value must be passed as a parameter
Yes: stored procedures always prevent injection
Yes: as long as the procedure runs under a database owner account
No: stored procedures cannot read user input at all
cards.explanation: What matters is whether input becomes part of the SQL text. A procedure that concatenates @ref into a string and executes it is exactly as vulnerable as the app was. Passing @ref as a bound parameter to the dynamic SQL, or avoiding dynamic SQL, fixes it.

cards.title: Dawn, and the board review
cards.setting: Bridge call, 6:05 am. The sky over Dubai is turning orange.

lines.text: Keystone has been back online since 4:02. Restored to 2:09:58 with the tail-log included. Data lost: none. Downtime: 1 hour 52 minutes, inside the RTO.
And the complaint form now uses parameterised queries and an account that can call one procedure. I've also set up alerts for injection patterns.
Then I owe you all breakfast. And the board will want to hear exactly this on Friday: the design, the queries, the performance, the recovery, the security.
Every stage we've cleared, in one meeting.
That's the final boss. Go-live review. You know everything you need. Let's show them.

cards.title: Midnight Vault secured
items: RPO is the most data you may lose; RTO is the longest you may be down. Backup frequency serves RPO, restore speed serves RTO.
Restore chain: tail-log if possible, latest full, latest differential, every later log in order. Stop at a point in time to undo a bad change.
Replicas, RAID and snapshots on the same storage are not backups. Keep separate, encrypted, immutable copies and test restores on a schedule.
Parameterised queries stop SQL injection; dynamic SQL inside procedures needs parameters too. Least privilege limits the damage.
Use TLS in transit, encryption at rest, salted slow hashes for secrets, masking for screens and test copies, and audit logs for insiders.
Data-protection laws worldwide share core principles: purpose, minimisation, retention, security and safeguards for transfers. Check the local law and sector rules before moving personal data.

cards.prompt: If your most important database failed tonight, how much data would you lose and how long would recovery take, honestly? When was the last time anyone proved it with a test restore?

quiz.question: The business agrees that OrvaPay may lose at most 5 minutes of transactions in a disaster. What is this number called?
options: The recovery time objective (RTO)
The backup retention period
The recovery point objective (RPO)
The mean time between failures
quiz.explanation: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time. RTO is how long the service may be down. Retention is how long backups are kept.

quiz.question: Keystone's RTO is 2 hours. A timed test restore of the full database, plus log replay, takes 5 hours. What does this tell you?
options: The RTO is met, because the data is fully recovered
The RTO cannot be met; a faster recovery path such as a standby is needed
The RPO must be changed to 5 hours
Nothing: test restores always run slower than real ones, so the target still holds
quiz.explanation: RTO is about how long the service is down. If recovery takes 5 hours against a 2-hour objective, the design fails the target and needs a faster path, or the business must formally accept a longer RTO. RPO concerns data loss, not time to recover.

quiz.question: Keystone takes a full backup on Sunday and a differential every night. Which backups are needed to restore to Thursday night's differential point?
options: Sunday's full backup and every differential from Monday to Thursday
Thursday's differential only
Every differential from Monday to Thursday, without the full backup
Sunday's full backup and Thursday's differential only
quiz.explanation: A differential contains all changes since the last full backup, so only the latest one is needed on top of the full. Incremental backups, by contrast, would all be needed in order. A differential cannot be restored without its full base.

quiz.question: After a failure, which restore sequence is correct for a database with full, differential and log backups?
options: Latest full, latest differential, then every later log in order
Latest differential, then latest full, then the most recent log backup
Every log backup since the database was created, then the full
Latest full, then every log backup, then the latest differential
quiz.explanation: Restores build forward from the full backup, add the latest differential, then replay all log backups taken after it, in sequence. The differential cannot come after the logs it predates, and skipping log files breaks the chain.

quiz.question: At 14:07:30 a support engineer runs DELETE FROM standing_orders without a WHERE clause on Keystone. Log backups run every 15 minutes, and the log is intact. What is the best recovery approach?
options: Restore last night's full backup over production to undo the delete
Restore a separate copy to 14:07:29 and move the deleted rows back
Fail over to the synchronous replica, which still has the rows
Wait for the next log backup, then roll it back
quiz.explanation: Point-in-time recovery to a separate copy, stopped just before the DELETE, recovers the rows without discarding everything else done since. Restoring last night's backup over production would lose a day's work, the replica has already applied the DELETE, and log backups cannot be 'rolled back' on their own.

quiz.question: Rafael says: 'We have a real-time replica in our disaster-recovery site, so we don't need backups.' What is the main flaw?
options: A replica copies mistakes and ransomware too, so it cannot go back in time
Replicas always run several hours behind, so the most recent data would be missing
Replicas cannot be located in another city
Replicas do not include indexes
quiz.explanation: Replication protects against losing a server or site, but a bad DELETE or encrypted data is copied within seconds. Backups give independent copies from earlier points in time. Both are needed.

quiz.question: Which change most reliably prevents SQL injection in the OrvaPay complaint search?
options: Strip single quotes from the input before building the SQL string
Use a parameterised query that binds the reference as data
Hide database error messages from users
Limit the input box to 20 characters
quiz.explanation: Parameterised queries keep the SQL text fixed and send input separately, so it can never become code. Stripping characters and length limits are fragile extra layers, and hiding errors helps but does not stop injection.

quiz.question: Layla's dashboard login needs to read summary figures. Which grant follows least privilege best?
options: SELECT on all tables in the database
SELECT on a few reporting views with only the needed columns
Membership of the database owner role
INSERT, UPDATE and SELECT on the summary tables so it can refresh them
quiz.explanation: Least privilege gives exactly what the task needs and no more. Narrow views limit which columns and rows are exposed. Read access to every table, owner rights or write rights all go beyond a read-only dashboard's needs.

quiz.question: The legacy wallet stored customer PINs encrypted with a key held by the app. Mei wants a better approach. What should Keystone store?
options: The PIN encrypted with a stronger key held by the app
A fast unsalted hash of the PIN
The PIN in plain text in a restricted table
A salted hash from a slow password-hashing algorithm
quiz.explanation: A secret that only needs to be verified should be hashed, not encrypted, so it cannot be decrypted by anyone with the key. A salt stops identical PINs giving identical hashes, and a slow algorithm makes guessing expensive. A fast unsalted hash of a short PIN is easy to brute force.

quiz.question: Call-centre agents need to confirm a caller's identity but should not see full national ID numbers, while the fraud team needs full values. Which control fits?
options: Dynamic masking by role, showing agents part of the ID number
Static masking of the production national ID column
Encryption at rest of the database files
Deleting ID numbers from the database after account opening is complete
quiz.explanation: Dynamic masking hides values at query time depending on the user's role, so agents see a partial ID number while authorised teams see it in full. Static masking would permanently change production data, encryption at rest does not affect what authorised users see, and deleting ID numbers breaks KYC duties.

bank.question: A telecom table bundle_subscriptions has key (msisdn, bundle_code, start_date) and columns end_date, bundle_price and subscriber_name. The bundle price is set per bundle code and the name belongs to the number's owner. Which columns break 2NF?
options: Only end_date, because its value can change after the bundle has started
Only subscriber_name, because names are not atomic
bundle_price and subscriber_name: each depends on part of the key
None, because a three-column key cannot have partial dependencies
bank.explanation: bundle_price depends on bundle_code alone and subscriber_name on msisdn alone: both are partial dependencies on a composite key, which 2NF forbids. end_date depends on the full subscription. Composite keys of any size can have partial dependencies.

bank.question: A table staff(emp_id PK, branch_id, branch_city, region_id, region_head) stores, for each employee, their branch, the branch's city, the branch's region and that region's head. What is the cleanest 3NF design?
options: staff(emp_id, branch_id, region_head); branches(branch_id, branch_city, region_id); regions(region_id)
staff(emp_id, branch_id, branch_city, region_id); regions(region_id, region_head); branches(branch_id)
staff(emp_id, branch_id); branches(branch_id, branch_city, region_id); regions(region_id, region_head)
One table per region, each holding staff and branch details
bank.explanation: Branch city and region depend on branch_id, and the region head depends on region_id, so both chains are transitive and need their own tables. The other two designs leave a transitive dependency in place (region_head or branch_city on staff), and splitting tables by region repeats structure without removing any dependency.

bank.question: Orvella's product rule: a customer can hold many accounts; an account can have up to four holders, exactly one marked PRIMARY. Which design captures this best in a relational model?
options: Columns holder1_id to holder4_id on accounts, with holder1 always treated as the primary holder and blanks allowed for the rest
A JSON array of holder ID numbers on accounts, validated by the mobile app before every save
A junction table with role and both foreign keys, plus database rules for the four-holder and one-primary limits
A primary_account_id column on customers plus a joint_flag on accounts to mark shared accounts
bank.explanation: The relationship is many-to-many, so it needs a junction table, and the role belongs to the pairing. Business limits such as 'at most four' and 'one primary' are then enforced in the database. Fixed holder columns are a repeating group, an app-validated JSON list bypasses the database, and one account per customer cannot model customers with many accounts.

bank.question: Operations cannot add the new Mombasa branch to the legacy system until its first account is opened, because branch details are stored only on account rows. What is the root cause, and what fixes it?
options: A delete anomaly; stop deleting closed accounts
An update anomaly; update all account rows whenever branch details change
A missing index on branch_id; add one so the branch can be found
An insert anomaly; give branches their own table keyed on branch_id
bank.explanation: Being unable to record one fact (a branch) until another exists (an account) is an insert anomaly, caused by facts about two entities sharing one table. Giving branches their own table removes it. An index speeds lookups but does not change what can be stored.

bank.question: A telco's subscribers table uses the mobile number (MSISDN) as its primary key. Numbers are recycled to new customers after a dormancy period. Billing history from the previous owner now appears under the new subscriber. What is the best redesign?
options: Keep MSISDN as the key but delete history when a number is recycled
Add the SIM serial number to the MSISDN to form a composite key
Prefix recycled numbers with an R so the key stays unique
A surrogate subscriber_id as key, with MSISDN as a dated attribute
bank.explanation: A natural key that changes owner over time is a poor primary key. A surrogate subscriber_id identifies the person permanently, and the number becomes a time-bounded attribute. Deleting history breaks retention and audit, SIM swaps would break a SIM-based key, and altering the number corrupts the real identifier.

bank.question: While merging duplicate customers, a script deletes the duplicate customer row. The foreign keys from accounts and transactions were declared ON DELETE CASCADE, and two years of transaction history disappear. What should the merge process have done?
options: Disable foreign keys during the merge so that deletes cannot cascade to child tables
Copy the transactions to a spreadsheet before running the merge
Delete transactions first so the cascade has nothing to remove
Re-point child rows to the surviving customer first, with deletes set to RESTRICT
bank.explanation: The safe merge moves every child reference to the surviving record and only then removes or flags the duplicate. A RESTRICT (or NO ACTION) rule makes the database refuse to delete a parent that still has children, which would have stopped this. Disabling keys or deleting history removes the very protection and data you need.

bank.question: An analyst stores customer mobile numbers such as 07700900123 in a BIGINT column to 'save space'. What problem appears first?
options: The leading zero is lost: 07700900123 becomes 7700900123
BIGINT cannot hold an 11-digit number, so the value overflows
Numbers cannot be searched with an equals condition
The column cannot have a UNIQUE constraint
bank.explanation: Numeric types drop leading zeros, so the stored value no longer matches the real number. Identifiers you never do arithmetic on, such as phone and national ID numbers, belong in text columns with a pattern check. BIGINT easily holds 11 digits, and numeric columns can be compared and made unique.

bank.question: Consider txn_detail(account_id, txn_date, amount, branch_id, branch_city) with key (account_id, txn_date). Each account belongs to one branch, and each branch is in one city. What is the highest normal form the table satisfies?
options: 1NF only, because branch_id depends on account_id alone
2NF, because every column depends on the whole key
3NF, because there are no repeating groups
BCNF, because the key is composite
bank.explanation: branch_id depends only on account_id, part of the composite key, so the table breaks 2NF and is in 1NF only. There is also a transitive dependency (branch_city on branch_id), but the lowest violation sets the highest form achieved.

bank.question: Finance reports that the sum of 10 wallet fees of USD 0.10 each is stored as 0.9999999999 in one system and 1.00 in another. Which column type explains the difference?
options: The first system uses DECIMAL with too many places; the second uses INTEGER
Both use FLOAT, but the second rounds on display only
System one uses binary floating point; system two uses exact DECIMAL
The first system stores amounts as text and converts them
bank.explanation: Binary floating point stores 0.10 approximately, so repeated addition drifts. DECIMAL stores exact base-10 values, so ten fees of 0.10 sum to exactly 1.00. This is why money columns should always use DECIMAL or NUMERIC.

bank.question: A call-detail table stores the tariff rate per minute at the time of each call, even though a tariffs table holds each package's current rate. A reviewer flags this as a 3NF violation. What is the best response?
options: It records the rate actually charged on that call, so it belongs there
The reviewer is right; remove the column and join to tariffs for every bill
The reviewer is right; keep the column but update it whenever tariffs change
It is acceptable only because the call table has a composite key
bank.explanation: The rate charged on a call is what the customer was billed at that moment. If the current tariff changes tomorrow, the old call must not change, so it is a different fact, not a duplicate. Joining to current tariffs or updating old rows would rewrite history and break billing disputes.

bank.question: Four accounts have balances of USD 10,000, NULL, USD 30,000 and USD 20,000. What does SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts return?
options: NULL, because one value is NULL
bank.explanation: AVG ignores NULLs: (10,000 + 30,000 + 20,000) / 3 = 20,000. USD 15,000 is what you would get by dividing the sum by all four rows, which would treat the unknown balance as zero.

bank.question: Five customers: A has 3 accounts, B has 1, C has 0, D has 2 and E has 0. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN account_holders return?
bank.explanation: A LEFT JOIN returns every match plus one row for each unmatched left row: 3 + 1 + 2 = 6 matched rows, plus 1 each for C and E = 8. An INNER JOIN would return 6.

bank.question: A branch has two accounts: account 1 (USD 500,000) has two joint holders and account 2 (USD 300,000) has one holder. A report joins accounts to account_holders and sums a.balance for the branch. What does it show, and why?
options: USD 800,000, because a join never changes totals
USD 1,300,000, because account 1 appears once per holder
USD 1,600,000, because every account is doubled
USD 1,100,000, because account 2 appears twice
bank.explanation: Joining to holders gives two rows for account 1 and one for account 2: 500,000 x 2 + 300,000 = 1,300,000. The true total is 800,000. Joint accounts are a classic source of fan-out in bank reporting.

bank.question: The board wants branches whose ATM withdrawals in October 2026 exceeded USD 5 million. Which query structure is correct?
options: WHERE SUM(amount) > 5000000 AND channel = 'ATM'; GROUP BY branch
WHERE channel and October dates; GROUP BY branch; HAVING SUM(amount) > 5000000
GROUP BY branch; HAVING channel = 'ATM' AND October dates; WHERE SUM(amount) > 5000000
WHERE channel = 'ATM'; GROUP BY branch, amount; HAVING amount > 5000000
bank.explanation: Row-level conditions (channel, dates) belong in WHERE, and the condition on the total belongs in HAVING after grouping by branch. Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE, and grouping by amount would produce one group per amount instead of per branch.

bank.question: There are 100 customers: 40 in Dubai, 45 in other cities and 15 with a NULL city. How many rows does WHERE city <> 'Dubai' return?
bank.explanation: For the 15 NULL rows, city <> 'Dubai' evaluates to UNKNOWN, so they are excluded along with the 40 Dubai rows, leaving 45. To include them, add OR city IS NULL.

bank.question: Vikram asks how many customers used instant payments at least once last month. Layla joins customers, account_holders and transactions, filters channel and dates, and uses COUNT(*). The result is 412,000, but the bank has only 260,000 wallet customers. What should she use?
options: COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id), because each customer repeats per transaction
COUNT(t.txn_id), because it skips the NULL transaction rows that inflate the count
SUM(1) instead of COUNT(*), because SUM is exact
COUNT(*) with a LEFT JOIN instead of an INNER JOIN
bank.explanation: After the join there is one row per transaction, so COUNT(*) counts transactions, not customers. COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) counts each customer once. COUNT(t.txn_id) and SUM(1) still count rows, and a LEFT JOIN would add customers with no instant-payment use.

bank.question: Which query correctly lists accounts that had no transactions at all during 2026?
options: LEFT JOIN transactions ON the account ID, with the 2026 date range and t.txn_id IS NULL both in WHERE
INNER JOIN transactions ON the account ID, WHERE txn_time < '2026-01-01'
LEFT JOIN transactions ON the account ID, WHERE t.txn_id IS NULL
LEFT JOIN transactions ON the account ID and the 2026 date range, then WHERE t.txn_id IS NULL
bank.explanation: The date range must restrict the match inside ON; then accounts with no 2026 match get NULLs and the anti-join keeps them. Putting the date in WHERE removes the NULL rows, so nothing qualifies. The plain anti-join without any date range finds accounts with no transactions ever, which misses accounts active only before 2026.

bank.question: Rafael runs SELECT with his WHERE clause and gets 4,812 rows. He then runs the UPDATE inside a transaction, and the database reports 48,213 rows affected. What should he do?
options: Commit, because the database knows better than the SELECT
Roll back, then find why the UPDATE's condition differs from the SELECT's
Commit, then run a second UPDATE that reverses the 43,401 rows that were not intended
Roll back, then run the UPDATE again outside a transaction
bank.explanation: A mismatch between the tested row count and the affected count means the statement is not doing what was intended. Rolling back undoes it completely. Committing and patching risks errors that cannot be fully reversed, and dropping the transaction removes the safety net.

bank.question: This query fails: SELECT branch_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM transactions WHERE total > 1000000 GROUP BY branch_id; What is the correct version of the filter?
options: Change WHERE total to WHERE SUM(total) > 1000000
Move the WHERE clause after GROUP BY without changing it
Move it to HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000000 after GROUP BY
Add total to the GROUP BY clause
bank.explanation: WHERE runs before grouping and before SELECT, so it can use neither the aggregate nor its alias. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Grouping by the alias is invalid, and WHERE must come before GROUP BY in any case.

bank.question: A report needs each account and its number of transactions in October, showing 0 for accounts with none. The query is accounts LEFT JOIN transactions (October condition in ON) GROUP BY account_id. Which expression gives the right count?
options: COUNT(*)
COUNT(a.account_id)
SUM(t.amount) / AVG(t.amount)
COUNT(t.txn_id)
bank.explanation: An account with no October transactions still produces one joined row with NULL transaction columns. COUNT(*) and COUNT(a.account_id) count that row as 1. COUNT(t.txn_id) skips the NULL and returns 0. The SUM/AVG ratio returns NULL for those accounts.

bank.question: Account 5501 has three transactions in time order: +5,000, -2,000 and +3,000. What does SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY txn_time) show on the third row?
bank.explanation: With ORDER BY in the window, SUM gives a running total: 5,000, then 3,000, then 6,000. 3,000 is just the third amount, and 10,000 adds the absolute values.

bank.question: Management wants to reward the 'top three positions' among 40 branches for instant-payment growth. Tied branches must share a position, and the next branch must take the next position number without gaps. Which function meets this rule?
options: RANK()
ROW_NUMBER()
NTILE(3)
DENSE_RANK()
bank.explanation: DENSE_RANK lets ties share a position and continues with the next number, so 'positions 1 to 3' can include more than three branches when there are ties. RANK skips numbers after ties, ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily, and NTILE splits rows into equal-sized buckets.

bank.question: A report computes LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY branch_id, month) to show month-on-month change per branch. Priya notices that the first month of the Lyon branch shows a huge drop. What is the cause?
options: LAG returns zero for the first row, so the change equals the whole monthly total
Ordering by two columns is not allowed in a window
LAG requires a GROUP BY on month
No PARTITION BY, so LAG takes another branch's last month as the prior month
bank.explanation: With no partition, the whole result is one window, so the row before Lyon's first month belongs to another branch. PARTITION BY branch_id ORDER BY month restarts the window at each branch, giving NULL (no prior month) instead of a false comparison.

bank.question: Risk wants accounts whose balance is above the average balance of their own branch, with the branch average shown. Which approach gives this in one pass over accounts?
options: WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts)
GROUP BY branch_id HAVING balance > AVG(balance)
AVG(balance) OVER (ORDER BY branch_id), filtered in the same query's WHERE clause
A partitioned AVG window in a CTE, then filter balance above it outside
bank.explanation: A partitioned window average gives each account its own branch's average on the same row, then an outer filter compares the two. The scalar subquery uses the bank-wide average, HAVING cannot see individual balances after grouping, and a window cannot be filtered in its own WHERE.

bank.question: Table blocked has 3 rows with customer_id values 101, 205 and NULL. Table customers has 1,000 customers, including 101 and 205. How many rows does SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked) return?
bank.explanation: For each customer not in the list, the test against NULL is UNKNOWN, so NOT IN is never TRUE and no row is returned. With NOT EXISTS, the answer would be 998.

bank.question: List A (instant-payment users) has 1,000 distinct customers and list B (card users) has 800 distinct customers; 150 customers are in both. How many rows does A UNION B return?
bank.explanation: UNION removes duplicates, so the 150 shared customers appear once: 1,000 + 800 - 150 = 1,650. UNION ALL would return 1,800.

bank.question: Customer Maria Santos moved from Mass to Premier in August. The warehouse's customer dimension simply overwrote her segment. What will a report of her April transactions by segment now show, and what design prevents it?
options: Her April transactions disappear; a type 1 dimension would keep them
Her April transactions stay under Mass, because facts store the segment
Her transactions split between both segments; a degenerate dimension prevents it
They appear under Premier; a type 2 dimension would keep them under Mass
bank.explanation: Overwriting (type 1) rewrites history: all facts now join to the Premier value. Type 2 adds a new row for the change, so April facts keep pointing to the Mass version and new facts point to Premier.

bank.question: A wallet fact table was built at the grain of 'one row per customer per day' with total amount and count. Product now asks for peak payment hours. What is the issue?
options: The date dimension needs an hour column added, which solves it
Daily grain has discarded the hour; a transaction-level fact table is needed
A window function over the daily facts can recover the hour each payment was made
The fact table needs a type 2 customer dimension
bank.explanation: Grain decides which questions a fact table can answer. Once facts are summed per day, the hour is gone and no dimension or window function can recover it. A transaction-level fact table, with a time-of-day dimension, supports hourly analysis.

bank.question: A telecom operator must store billions of call detail records a month, written continuously and queried mostly by subscriber and time range. Which NoSQL family is designed for this pattern?
options: Graph database
Document store
Key-value cache
Wide-column store
bank.explanation: Wide-column stores are built for very high write volumes and queries by partition key and time, which fits call detail records. Graph databases optimise relationship traversal, document stores flexible records, and caches fast lookups of small values.

bank.question: OrvaPay replicates wallet balances across two data centres with eventual consistency. A customer with USD 10,000 sends USD 8,000 from one phone and, within a second, USD 7,000 from another, each request reaching a different data centre. What is the main risk, and what is the right control?
options: Both can pass on a stale balance; the debit needs one strongly consistent ACID ledger
The second transfer is delayed by a few seconds; a faster network fixes it
The balances converge a few seconds later, so no money is lost; a nightly report can flag gaps
One data centre crashes; add a third replica
bank.explanation: Under eventual consistency each replica may approve a debit against a balance that does not yet reflect the other, so the wallet is overspent by USD 5,000. Convergence later does not undo the payments. Money movements need a single source of truth with atomic, isolated checks.

bank.question: OrvaPay's two most frequent queries are WHERE wallet_id = ? AND txn_time >= ? (statement) and WHERE wallet_id = ? (balance history). Which single index serves both best?
options: (txn_time, wallet_id)
(txn_time)
(wallet_id, txn_time)
(amount, wallet_id)
bank.explanation: With wallet_id first, both queries can seek on the leading column, and the first also uses txn_time for the range. With txn_time first, an equality filter on wallet_id alone cannot use the index efficiently.

bank.question: A statement query filters on wallet_id with an index on (wallet_id, txn_time). The plan shows an index seek followed by 5,000 key lookups into the table to fetch amount and channel. What change most reduces the work?
options: Add a separate index on amount
Rebuild the table as a heap without a clustered index
Make the index covering by including amount and channel
Rewrite the query with SELECT * so all columns come together
bank.explanation: Key lookups happen because the index lacks columns the query needs. Including them makes the index covering, so the query is answered from the index alone. A separate amount index does not help this filter, and SELECT * would need even more lookups.

bank.question: Call-centre agents search customers by the last four digits of their mobile number with WHERE mobile LIKE '%4567'. It scans 30 million rows. Which fix allows an index seek?
options: Add a normal B-tree index on mobile
Change the condition to LIKE '%4567%'
Index a column holding the last four digits and search it with equals
Store mobile as an integer so the comparison becomes numeric and faster
bank.explanation: A B-tree on mobile is sorted from the first digit, so a leading wildcard cannot seek. A derived, indexed last-four column turns the search into an equality seek. A wider wildcard is worse, and converting the type does not help a suffix search.

bank.question: Column national_id is VARCHAR(12) with an index. The query WHERE national_id = 880312456789 (no quotes) scans the table. What is the cause?
options: National ID values are too long to be indexed
Comparing text with a number converts every row, which blocks the seek
The index on a VARCHAR column is only used by LIKE conditions, never by equals
VARCHAR columns cannot be compared with equals
bank.explanation: When the types differ, the engine typically converts the column side to match the number, so it cannot seek. Writing the literal as text ('880312456789') keeps the comparison sargable.

bank.question: A month-end query's plan shows the optimiser estimated 12 rows from a filter but 2.4 million actually came back, and it chose a nested-loop join that ran for an hour. What is the most likely cause and first fix?
options: The table needs a clustered index on every column
The server is short of memory, so adding more RAM should be the first fix to try
Stale statistics misled the optimiser; update them and re-check the plan
Nested-loop joins are always wrong; disable them for the database
bank.explanation: A large gap between estimated and actual rows usually means the optimiser is using outdated statistics, leading to a plan suited to tiny inputs. Refreshing statistics often fixes the plan. Hardware and disabling join types treat symptoms.

bank.question: A compliance report counts transactions above USD 10,000 twice within one transaction. Between the two counts, a teller commits a new USD 30,000 deposit, so the second count is one higher. Which problem is this?
options: A phantom read
A dirty read
A lost update
A deadlock
bank.explanation: New rows appearing in a repeated range query, because another transaction committed an insert, is a phantom read. A dirty read involves uncommitted data, and a lost update involves overwritten writes.

bank.question: Keystone's month-end profit calculation reads every account for 40 minutes and must see one consistent point in time, but tellers must keep posting transactions without being blocked. Which approach fits best?
options: A snapshot (MVCC) isolation level, so it reads one consistent point without blocking writers
Read uncommitted, so the calculation takes no locks at all
Serializable isolation, holding locks on every account until the calculation finishes
Read committed, accepting that some balances will change during the 40-minute run, as they would anyway
bank.explanation: Row versioning lets a reader see the database as it was when its snapshot began, while writers continue. Read uncommitted gives dirty, inconsistent data; serializable locking would block tellers for 40 minutes; read committed would mix values from different moments.

bank.question: OrvaPay's transfer procedure updates the sender's wallet, then the receiver's. When Lucas pays Mina while Mina pays Lucas, deadlocks occur. Which redesign removes the cause?
options: Update the receiver first, then the sender
Update the two wallets in a fixed order, such as lower wallet_id first
Commit after the sender's update and start a new transaction for the receiver
Lower the isolation level to read uncommitted
bank.explanation: The deadlock is a cycle created by opposite lock orders. A fixed global order makes cycles impossible. Receiver-first just mirrors the problem, splitting the transaction breaks atomicity, and isolation level does not change write locks.

bank.question: A wallet top-up starts a transaction, locks the customer's row, then sends an OTP and waits up to two minutes for the customer to enter it before committing. On busy days many requests time out. What is the root cause?
options: Locks are held while waiting for the customer, blocking others for minutes
OTPs are too short to be secure
The isolation level is too low, so concurrent top-ups keep overwriting each other
The wallet table has too many indexes
bank.explanation: Transactions should be short and must never wait on a human. Verify the OTP first, then open the transaction, apply the change and commit in milliseconds. Holding locks for minutes causes blocking and timeouts.

bank.question: A customer double-taps 'Pay' on a weak mobile signal, and the app sends the same payment request twice with the same request ID. Which database control ensures it is processed once?
options: A UNIQUE constraint on the request ID, so the second insert fails
A CHECK constraint that amount is greater than zero
A foreign key from payments to wallets
A non-unique index on request ID, so duplicates are found quickly afterwards
bank.explanation: An idempotency key enforced by a UNIQUE constraint lets the first request succeed and makes the duplicate fail, so the app can return the original result. A CHECK, a foreign key or a non-unique index all allow two identical payments.

bank.question: Keystone's RPO is 15 minutes. Log backups run every 30 minutes, on the hour and half hour. At 16:20 the server fails and the log file cannot be read. How much data is lost, and is the RPO met?
options: About 15 minutes, so the RPO is exactly met
About 30 minutes, the log backup interval, so the RPO is not met
About 20 minutes (16:00 to 16:20), so the RPO is not met
Nothing, because the replica holds the rest
bank.explanation: The last usable log backup ended at 16:00 and no tail-log backup is possible, so 20 minutes of work is lost, which exceeds 15. With 30-minute log backups the worst case is 30 minutes, so the schedule cannot meet a 15-minute RPO by design.

bank.question: Schedule: full backup Sunday 23:00; differentials daily at 23:00 Monday to Saturday; log backups every hour at 30 minutes past. The server fails on Thursday at 09:45, and a tail-log backup succeeds. Which set restores with the least data loss and the fewest files?
options: Sunday full, Monday to Wednesday differentials, then the tail-log
Sunday full, Wednesday 23:00 differential, the 11 log backups from 23:30 to 09:30, then the tail-log
Wednesday 23:00 differential on its own, then the 11 log backups from 23:30 to 09:30 and the tail-log
Sunday full, Wednesday 23:00 differential, then the tail-log only
bank.explanation: The latest differential covers everything since Sunday, so earlier differentials are not needed. All log backups after it (23:30, then 00:30 to 09:30: 11 files) must be applied in order before the tail-log. A differential cannot be restored without its full backup, and skipping the log backups breaks the chain.

bank.question: Ransomware attackers gain domain admin rights at a manufacturer and encrypt the database servers, then delete the backups on the network backup share, which used the same admin accounts. Which control would most likely have saved the data?
options: An immutable or offline copy managed under separate credentials
A synchronous replica in a second data centre
Daily full backups instead of weekly ones, kept on the same backup share
RAID 6 instead of RAID 5 on the database servers
bank.explanation: Attackers with admin rights can delete anything those rights reach. An immutable or offline copy with separate credentials survives. A replica would copy the encryption, more frequent backups on the same share would also be deleted, and RAID only protects against disk failure.

bank.question: Keystone's database is 2 TB. A full restore runs at 400 GB per hour, and log replay plus integrity checks take another hour. The RTO is 4 hours. What is the conclusion?
options: About 5 hours for the restore itself, so the 4-hour RTO is met within tolerance
About 3 hours, so the RTO is met
The RTO cannot be judged without knowing the RPO
About 6 hours, so the RTO is missed and a standby or faster restore is needed
bank.explanation: 2,000 GB / 400 GB per hour = 5 hours, plus 1 hour = 6 hours, which exceeds the 4-hour RTO. Meeting it needs a different approach, such as a standby that can take over, or the business must accept a longer RTO. RPO is a separate target.

bank.question: A procedure searches complaints with: SET @sql = 'SELECT * FROM complaints WHERE ref = ''' + @ref + ''''; then executes @sql. The app calls the procedure with a bound parameter. Is the system protected against injection?
options: Yes: binding the parameter in the app protects every statement that runs downstream of it
Yes: stored procedures always run input as data
No: the only fix is to remove the procedure and use an ORM
No: @ref is pasted into dynamic SQL inside the procedure, so it needs a parameter there too
bank.explanation: The app binding protects the call to the procedure, but inside it the value is pasted into SQL text and executed, recreating the injection. Executing the dynamic SQL with @ref as a bound parameter (or avoiding dynamic SQL) fixes it. An ORM is one option, not the only one.

bank.question: A developer needs to correct 200 mis-posted fees in Keystone's production database. What is the best practice?
options: Give the developer temporary database owner rights for the day
A reviewed script under an approved ticket, run and logged by an authorised account
Let the developer run the fix from their own login, since they wrote the code
Ask the developer to share their script on WhatsApp so the DBA can run it immediately
bank.explanation: Separation of duties keeps people who write code from changing production data directly. An approved, reviewed script run by an authorised account leaves an audit trail. Temporary owner rights and direct developer access bypass control, and informal channels lose the record.

bank.question: Keystone uses transparent data encryption (TDE). An attacker steals the password of the reporting service account and downloads customer data through normal queries. Why did TDE not prevent this, and what would have limited the damage?
options: TDE was misconfigured, since properly configured TDE blocks every unauthorised query on its own
TDE decrypts for any valid login; least privilege and column encryption or masking limit it
TDE only protects indexes; encrypting the tables as well would have stopped it
TDE protects data in transit only; enabling TLS would have stopped it
bank.explanation: Encryption at rest protects files, disks and backups from being read outside the database. A valid login sees plain data. Limiting what the account can query, and protecting the most sensitive columns with encryption or masking, reduces what a stolen credential exposes.

bank.question: An audit finds a legacy table storing wallet PINs as unsalted MD5 hashes, and many rows share identical hash values. What is the risk, and what is the fix?
options: MD5 hashes can be decrypted with the server's key, so the key must be rotated at once
Equal PINs share hashes and are easy to crack; re-hash with a salted slow algorithm
There is no risk, because hashes cannot be reversed
The hashes take too much space; store the PINs encrypted instead
bank.explanation: Without a salt, equal PINs give equal hashes, and fast hashes of short PINs are easy to look up or brute force. Salted, slow password-hashing algorithms fix both. Hashes have no key, and encryption would make the PINs recoverable.

bank.question: Orvella Bank wants to send full customer records to an overseas cloud analytics vendor for a churn model. What should the data team do first?
options: Send the data, because the vendor's signed contract already includes a strict confidentiality clause
Send the data, as long as it is encrypted in transit
Check the regulator's cloud and outsourcing rules and the data law on transfers, get approvals, and minimise the data
Refuse, because data-protection laws forbid personal data from ever leaving a country
bank.explanation: Regulated firms must check the current regulator requirements for outsourcing and cloud use, and the data-protection rules on cross-border transfers, and get any approvals before sending customer data abroad, sending only what the purpose needs. A contract or TLS alone does not meet these duties, and most laws restrict transfers with safeguards rather than banning them outright.

bank.question: Marketing wants to keep every customer's ID document images indefinitely 'in case they are useful for AI later'. Which response reflects sound data-protection practice?
options: Keep everything, because storage is cheap and the data may be valuable
Keep it only for defined purposes and the required retention period, then delete or anonymise
Delete ID document images immediately after account opening
Move the images to a cheaper archive tier and keep them there indefinitely in case of future use
bank.explanation: Purpose limitation and retention mean holding personal data only as long as a defined purpose and legal record-keeping duties require. Deleting immediately could breach KYC retention rules, and keeping or archiving indefinitely for vague future use increases risk without justification.
